QUERY RESPECTING FREEZE ON DEVELOPMENT OF NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. I will not continue to ask what he is going to do tomorrow, because clearly he is not going to tell the Canadian people and the House of Commons until tomorrow. What I would like to do instead is to go back to a question and answer of last Monday, which the Prime Minister will recall. Looking at the past in 1978, as reported in Hansard for June 14, 1982, the Prime Minister said:
I did advocate the policy of suffocation, which is a freeze, but that policy was always advocated in a bilateral context-
And the Prime Minister told us that that policy was not accepted by either of the two major powers.
In his speech in Madrid, the Prime Minister said that he would be advocating a freeze on the development of new nuclear weapons. Was he saying that he would lend his support and the support of Canada to the freeze movement now taking place, which is asking for a bilateral, verifiable freeze on the development of new nuclear weapons?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING FREEZE ON DEVELOPMENT OF NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will have to answer that question in at least the same length as it was asked. The 1978 position was the advocation of a suffocation on new weapons, which it is perfectly justifiable to call a freeze on new weapons. That proposal, as the previous questioner pointed out, was not accepted by either of the super powers. On the contrary, since that speech was made, the Soviet Union has not suffocated new arms, it has deployed 300 SS-20s, each with a capacity of three warheads. That is what happened since I made my futile plea for a freeze. That has changed the strategic balance. The policy that NATO is following now is the re-establishment of the balance, and the freeze should continue on all other weapons.
As to the SS-20s, the NATO decision is a two-track one. It is on the one hand to be prepared to deploy Cruise and Pershing II missiles, which are a year and a half down the road at the soonest, but to hope that the threat or the possibility of deploying those missiles to counter the SS-20s will be enough to convince the Soviet Union to go either for the zero option proposed by the United States-no intermediate-range nuclear arms-or, alternatively, to negotiate a very, very reduced level of such arms. That is the position of the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Madam Speaker, I obviously cannot speak for Mr. Peckford or speculate on what he has in mind. I can tell the hon. member that we never left the negotiating table. Mr. Peckford refused to meet with us on February 16, as had been requested, and decided to go to court instead. He has refused negotiations ever since.
I had a meeting with Mr. Marshall a few weeks ago. I asked him whether he would come to the negotiating table, but was turned down. He agreed to meet with me, only on the basis that it would not be a negotiating session but simply a discussion. Therefore, the federal government has been at the negotiating table all along. We never left it.
If Mr. Peckford or his representatives want to come back to the negotiating table, they will find us there. We have been waiting for them. We have never said that we refuse to negotiate while the matter is before the courts. We are quite ready to negotiate. In fact, we indicated quite clearly, as we did with Nova Scotia, that we are ready to arrive at an agreement that will withstand any court decision, one that cannot be changed by whatever court decision might be rendered eventually.
The record is straight. It speaks for itself. We are quite ready to negotiate. We have always been ready to negotiate. The ones who left the negotiating table are the representatives of the Government of Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: MR. ROSE-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF "PROTECTED PERSONS"
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. 1 seek to put a question for clarification. With the greatest respect, I seek Madam Speaker's ruling about the role of hon. members in the matter of "protected persons" as described in Bcauchesne's fifth edition, Citation 321.
The reason I seek this clarification is that yesterday the member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) was named by Your Honour for using unparliamentary language and was removed from the House following his attempt to set the record straight on a matter of consequence, at least to Mr. Justice Thomas Berger. Yet on Tuesday the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) twice described the conduct of Mr. Justice Berger as reprehensible. Madam Speaker, Citation 428 of Erskine May cites the following passage; it is in the footnote on page 428:
Mr. Speaker ruled that... reflections on a judge's character or motives cannot be made except on a motion, nor can any charge of a personal nature be made except on a motion.
Clearly, Madam Speaker, the minister's remarks were not by way of motion but in answer to an hon. member's question. Describing a judge's conduct as reprehensible is bound to be construed as a reflection on the judge's character and, according to the precedents I have cited, perhaps the judge deserved the protection of the Chair-or other hon. members-under Beauchesne Citation 321 or May at page 428.
1 would be grateful if Your Honour would be so kind as to consider the points I have raised and later, perhaps, inform the House as to the duties of both hon. members and the Chair in cases such as this in order to end the confusion or any possible inference of double standards.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

subsubtopic: MR. ROSE-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF "PROTECTED PERSONS"

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBY-REMARKS OF MR. CHRETIEN RESPECTING DONALD MARSHALL CASE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a longstanding practice in this place that, as a matter of courtesy, when an hon. member intends to raise a question of privilege reflecting upon the conduct of another hon. member, the hon. member against whom allegations are about to be made should be in his place in the House.
I strongly suggest it would be most inappropriate and certainly not in keeping with the long-standing practices of this place to raise a question of privilege reflecting on the conduct of a member who is not here to hear the allegations. I suggest there is every right and every obligation to set the question over until the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) is in his place.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBY-REMARKS OF MR. CHRETIEN RESPECTING DONALD MARSHALL CASE
speechtext:
In my time I have heard questions of privilege in the absence of hon. members involved in those questions of privilege. I am very careful not to give rulings in the House unless the hon. members involved are in the House.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) will know that question of privilege is a matter that is very, very urgent and that I am justified in telling the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) that since it is an urgent matter, he probably would want to raise it immediately. 1 am suggesting that he probably would want to raise it immediately, and I am ready to hear him today. If he wants to defer, that is fine with me, I will wait; but it seems to me somewhat contradictory that an urgent question of privilege can be deferred one day or even a couple of hours. However, if the hon. member wants to defer, 1 will be patient with him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBY-REMARKS OF MR. CHRETIEN RESPECTING DONALD MARSHALL CASE
speechtext:
It is not that it is not a question of urgency, with the greatest of respect. The practice is that a question of privilege, particularly one of this nature which deals with personalities, should be raised at the earliest opportunity. The earliest fitting and proper opportunity is when the minister is in the House, since the question deals with reflections on his personal conduct as a minister.
1 would advise my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), to defer the question until such time as the minister is in the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBY-REMARKS OF MR. CHRETIEN RESPECTING DONALD MARSHALL CASE
speechtext:

The one whose privilege is affected, of course, is the first one who is concerned, and in his view it is supposed to be so urgent that we stop all business of the House because we must consider that question of privilege. That is the basic principle behind questions of privilege.
Does the hon. member want to defer? If he wants to defer, that is fine; I will wait.

That this House condemns the Government, and in particular, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, for its failure to meet any of the objectives for which the Government continues to seek authority to spend in excess of one billion dollars in this fiscal year on behalf of Canada's aboriginal peoples, for its tolerance of the miserable conditions existing in native communities throughout Canada which are of a standard vastly inferior to those found in most Third World countries, for the minister's failure to exercise his obligatory trust responsibility, and for the minister's contempt of Parliament as manifested by his deliberate refusal to comply with the statutory obligations which legally require him to report to the House on the progress of the implementation of the James Bay agreement.

Madam Speaker, you may well ask, and we may well be questioned by our friends opposite and by people who watch us through the window to the outside today, why we would use a whole day of precious parliamentary time, when the country is in such serious economic difficulties, to discuss matters relating to the affairs of our native people. I would rather look at it as discussing a favourite subject of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-the North-South dialogue, except that this dialogue is more of a domestic nature.
I shall not have any difficulty explaining to you, or to anyone who is watching, why this has become such an urgent problem. It is urgent because the burden of economic difficulties that we must all suffer in times like these is unequally distributed in the country. A disproportionate load of the economic misery which this government has bestowed on the Canadian people is borne by the poor. And most native people in this country, Mr. Speaker, are among the poorest of the poor.
We talk about high unemployment, but in most native communities the unemployment rate is not 15 or 20 per cent, it is 95 per cent. Despite a whole series of royal commissions and studies over the last two or three decades into the housing conditions in the native communities, the housing situation is deplorable. It is not even comparable to conditions which exist in some Third World countries.
This debate is urgent because the conditions in which our native people live have attracted the attention of the world
June 17, 1982

outside. International tribunals such as the World Health Organization, world courts and human rights fora are dealing with the problems of the native people in Canada. Our image as a nation which espouses certain fundamental values in terms of the human condition is being blemished. It is urgent because the government is embarking on a new phase of the implementation of its Indian affairs policy which, when completed, will have the most profound effect and consequences on our native people. It is also urgent because there is a requirement under the first part of the constitutional accord to hold conferences within one year with provincial premiers and officials to determine once and for all the role and place of our native people within the framework of our new basic law and our new charter of rights.
I do not wish to overdramatize this question but some people are asking why it is that we impose economic sanctions on countries like South Africa because of the way they treat their native people when standards of health care and education for our own natives are, in the main, very much inferior to those found in South Africa.
Some people will be offended by what I have to say today. Many people find it easy to practise virtue from a distance and manage to overlook what is occurring in their own backyard. They will say that it is not fair to make the comparison with South Africa because, after all, our native people were declared persons 30 years ago. Ten years after that they were given the right to vote by the Right Hon. George Diefenbaker.
We consider it urgent, nevertheless, when one small segment of our society finds itself totally isolated from the mainstream of life. We hear reports of life-threatening situations which exist in our native communities, and our jails are overcrowded with native persons whose only relief from frustration is alcohol and crime.
We want to talk about all these things today, and my colleagues will place on the record in some detail statistics and facts of which we should all be ashamed. On the surface, as I have said, our Indian people have all the rights society grants its citizens, or at least so it seems when one looks back over history. There are, however, some very essential differences. For instance, when an ordinary Canadian goes to the polls he elects a government; an Indian person elects himself a trustee. The ordinary Canadian in a provincial election chooses a government or representative most able to manage such things as health care, education, and community services. But the Indian on the reserve has to rely on the federal government to provide him with these things. The provinces redistribute money they have collected in taxes to municipalities and individuals in the form of per capita grants and contributions to sustain community infrastructures. But when such payments are made by the federal government on behalf of the native people, the average Canadian usually considers that to be welfare.
There are other factors which set native people apart from us. Our registered Indians cannot buy and sell their houses without the consent of the minister. They cannot start a
Supply
business without such consent. If the band to which they belong has any property or assets, then the band cannot sell or convert them without the consent of the trustee, which is the federal minister. If consent is given to, say, sell land or resources belonging to Indian people under their treaty, the money is put in a trust fund maintained and controlled by the minister. That trust fund presently contains between $500 million and $600 million, which will grow to $1 billion by 1985. Incidentally, the government, of course, uses this money and pays a rate of interest 3 per cent or 4 per cent below that which it currently pays in the marketplace. I asked the minister in the House why it is that he cheats our native people of $30 million a year. I have been fighting for a year on behalf of the Fort Nelson Indian band to get the minister either to release the funds or pay a decent rate of interest. The fight is still going on and I hope the minister takes note and will remember that I will not be giving up.
There is a special trust fund for minors which the minister administers, presumably because Indian parents are not considered trustworthy to care for their own children. We have heard evidence before the committee of children for whom such trust moneys are kept in the minister's pocket here in Ottawa while they go to school hungry every day.
Such are the rights of our native people, Mr. Speaker, and such is their equality before our law. It is that trust responsibility which the minister has under the act and the way it is being discharged which I wish to examine in greater detail a little later. First let me give you an overview of the situation to which we generally refer as Indian affairs.
Under the new Constitution Indians, Inuit and Metis, all non-status Indians, are all referred to in one general category: aboriginal people. There are about 300,000 registered Indians who are governed under a special statute known as the Indian Act. The Inuit are specifically excluded from this act, but because of a 1939 court decision the minister had to assume some jurisdiction and responsibility for the Inuit people as well. By far the largest category of aboriginal people are the so-called Metis or non-status Indians. We think, although no one knows for sure, that they number in excess of one million.
The issue of the Metis, as far as the federal government is concerned, was settled during the Riel rebellion. The nonstatus Indians have, through bureaucratic commission or omission, never obtained or never lost their status. They are administered by the provinces, and in most cases are even worse off than their counterparts on reserves. In some cases they live on the reserves and share the same house with brothers and sisters. Under the treaties made with the Indians they were allowed to select certain lands, in most cases up to 160 acres per person, which could not be alienated or expropriated nor made subject to taxation, although much of this land has, of course, been alienated and expropriated over the years and some bands have never selected their lands. But that which is owned by the Indians and held in trust by the minister amounts in the aggregate, south of the 60th parallel, to an area the size of Nova Scotia.

These lands, even though they lie within the provinces, are not provincial lands. The resources, both surface and subsurface, are not provincial resources and the people who live on them are not governed by a provincial government. They are citizens, some argue, of a third territory who have the distinction of not being represented in Parliament. I should perhaps qualify that by saying that they are represented by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). We must assume the reason for this is that Indians are not capable of representing themselves. However, we look at the minister's mandate to represent our first citizens as part of his trust responsibility as well.
There is a lot of misunderstanding around, Mr. Speaker, even among our own colleagues here in the House, about the responsibilities we and the minister have for our aboriginal people. What is more, we believe that even the present trustee and his colleagues in cabinet are not certain what their responsibilities are. Let me quote from the report of the Auditor General who had difficulty determining what the minister's trust responsibilities were as well. In his last report he says:
For example, managers posed the following questions: is the role of the department one of prescription, where resources are allocated according to priorities interpreted by the department, or is it one of support, where the allocation is based on priorities determined by native people? Is it some of each and should the mix vary from one native group to another? Is the department accountable for producing social and economic gains for the native people, or is it responsible simply for ensuring an equitable distribution of financial support as native groups pursue their own objectives? Responses to these kinds of questions would have implications for accountability and control within the department.
Further on he said:
We therefore concluded that the direction given to the Department concerning its relationship with native people was not sufficiently clear to identify what DIAND should be accountable for in relation to its mandate. We also found little evidence to indicate that the Department had tried to clarify its accountability to Parliament by making assumptions in regard to its mandate, developing corresponding objectives and seeking approval for them.
The minister, in response to a question I asked him on May 13 concerning the Musqueam Indian situation in Vancouver, said this:
It is the fundamental principle of whether the minister has a trust responsibility, which is a key question to the Indian community in Canada.
He says it is a question whether the minister has that responsibility; he does not even know. He goes on:
That is what is involved in this particular case. I think some Indian leaders to whom I have talked realize that this fundamental question which has been a source of frustration to everyone concerned for so many years will have to be determined.
It is for that reason that he is putting the Musqueam people of Vancouver through the Supreme Court at a likely cost to them of $1 million. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you would not permit me the time to give a very precise historical and legal overview of the various acts, statutes and Royal proclamations which establish the special rights Inuits and Indians have, and what they are. But there is really no longer any doubt that special rights do exist, and the various instruments by which they were established have been badly bruised and injured and offended.
There is one general understanding which distorts the perception most Canadians have of the problem, and that has
to do with the treaties we have made with the Indians in the past. None of them were treaties of surrender; rather, they were arrangements for co-existence and friendship. The Indians were never conquered. They never surrendered. They signed arrangements and contracts for co-existence. At no time did the Indians agree to give up land to which they always considered themselves spiritually attached. Instead the treaties were viewed as a guarantee that as long as the sun shines, the grass grows, the rivers flow and nature celebrates its cycles, they shall at all times be part of those cycles.
I want to quote briefly from a report of treaty commissioners who negotiated Treaty No. 8, which was made June 21, 1899. The commissioners said:
Our chief difficulty was the apprehension that the hunting and fishing privileges were to be curtailed. The provision in the treaty under which ammunition and twine is to be furnished went far in the direction of quieting the fears of the Indians, for they admitted that it would be unreasonable to furnish the means of hunting and fishing if laws were to be enacted which would make hunting and fishing so restricted as to render it impossible to make a livelihood by such pursuit. But over and above the provision, we had to solemnly assure them that only such laws as to hunting and fishing as were in the interest of the Indians ... would be made .. . and that they would be as free to hunt and fish after the treaty as they would be if they never entered into it.
Such is the nature of these treaties, and there cannot be any doubt about that. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the courts have come to grips with the situation and in the main agree with the native people about that.
We all know what happened to these treaties. All of us must share part of the blame. We have not had the courage to admit that what has been done in the past was wrong. Nor have we had the compassion or the will to set it right. Maybe I should qualify that by stating that we have never been stingy in providing sufficient financial resources to set this inequity right, or to solve any problems the Indian people have if money were a solution to these problems. In fact, the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has a budget which exceeds $1 billion a year to carry out his mandate. That is $4,000 for every man, woman and child under his care. In the case of a family of five, that amounts to $20,000. That excludes the Metis and non-status Indians. While that would normally be sufficient to sustain an ordinary family above the poverty line, the paternalistic system and a ravenous bureaucratic monster administering these funds is not only gobbling up the lion's share of the money, but in the process has gobbled up any self-esteem, any self-reliance and even some of the most basic freedoms and rights that our native peoples once thought they had. It has rendered the Indians totally dependent upon the welfare system.
Let me give a few examples in terms of numbers to show the enormity of the problem. Overall, in the department of Indian Affairs-and the minister is responsible for a couple of other departments as well-there are 4,463 people. This includes Indian agents and people who help to carry out his mandate. Despite the fact that Indians have taken over or are supposed
June 17, 1982

to be taking over many of the programs which were formerly administered by the department itself, the number of people increased by 308 over the last two years. The over-all cost of the minister's administration is $1.1 billion. That is over $1,000 million to administer the affairs of 250,000 people.
The Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, in the course of examining this year's estimates, which, incidentally, led to the drafting of its now infamous fifth report which was tabled in the House and on which this motion is generally based, singled out one of the regions for closer scrutiny and special consideration. Because of a number of problems which are peculiar to British Columbia, some of which my colleagues will touch upon, the committee held two days of hearings in Vancouver examining the affairs of the B.C. region. This region stands out for two main reasons. First, most of the province was not covered by a treaty. Treaty commissioners did not cover the province as they did the prairie provinces. Treaty aid covers almost all of northern British Columbia.
Second, most of the bands and tribal councils in British Columbia have reached such a high degree of self-reliance that the departmental services and interventions are no longer required or wanted. In fact, there is duplication of some services, if not outright competition for some of the programs between departmental officials and some of the bands. Despite that fact, the region employs 557 people who are organized within ten major departments.
I have with me a brief overview of how the department of Indian affairs functions. First we have the department of the director general which has four staff members. The average salary amounts to $35,000 or $36,000. Incidentally, this department spent $63,223 on travel between April, 1981 and January 11, 1982.
Next is the department called director of local government which has 13 staff members who earn an average salary of $30,000. That group of 13 people spent $109,457 on travel between April, 1981 and January 11, 1982.
Next I will mention the director of the socio-economic development department. He and his 21 staff members earn an average salary of $30,000. They spent only $94,000 on travel in the same period.
The next department is that of the personnel manager who has 18 staff members. They have an average salary of $25,000 and spent $32,000 on travel in the same period.
Then we come to the engineering and architecture department which has 23 engineers and architects in the B.C. region. But the 23 engineers and architects have spent $119,674 in travel between April, 1981 and January 11, 1982. What I have mentioned comprises just the executive branch. There are in total 171 people who work in the British Columbia regional office.
We have many horror stories like this that we would like to place on the record today. The bureaucrats are in competition with the Indians for programs. They are in this bureaucratic game of "save your job and build your ivory tower". So fierce is the competition for control that it eats up most of the resources available to the region, to the point where those
Supply
bands who experience 95 per cent unemployment, abject poverty and human deprivation of the worst kind are left out almost completely.
The minister might want to dispute these figures, but we have a document that comes from the minister's own regional office in Vancouver. It shows the per capita distribution of funds in the region. The document is entitled "Department of Indian Affairs Contribution to Band Councils, 1981-1982". One band in northern British Columbia has received $36 per capita; yet another band received $4,087. There is no norm. There is no rule. There is nothing. There are no guidelines. There are no standards or minimum requirements for community infrastructure. There are Indian villages everywhere in Canada in 1982 which are taking into account such factors as climate and that are infinitely worse off than some of the poorest settlements in the Third World countries. Often they have no electricity or water distribution or even the most basic sanitary facilities. I can take you, Mr. Speaker, to places in my riding where three generations of one family live in one room not bigger than a living room in the average home. They suffer temperatures of 40 degrees below zero with the only source of heat a converted oil drum as a stove. There is no television and no money to buy batteries for the transistor radio.
What does that do to our national pride? Are we the same people who parade around the world promoting North-South dialogue, the champions of the Third World? I make no apologies at all for taking the time of the House today to speak about these problems.
As I said earlier, there are some bands and individuals who have the ears and the attention of the bureaucrats. We heard from the Indian affairs Mafia in British Columbia. Of course, we do not call them that, but some of the Indian people with whom we have come in contact call them that. The interpretation of the word "Mafia" as it relates to the British Columbia Indian region means Members Against the Firing of Indian Agents. We heard in committee of an individual who at one time received a $300,000 loan to start a personal business. The business was not designed to create any employment or jobs. It was a trailer court, his own personal business. An official of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development told the minister right from the outset that this particular loan was intended to be a personal retirement fund for the individual. The loan was made at preferred rates of interest to start the business. When he failed to meet his other obligations and failed to repay the principal and interest under the loan, he was given another $300,000, except this time it was in the form of a gift. The second $300,000 was to help him over the hurdle. My colleague, the hon. member for Okanagan-Similk-ameen (Mr. King), will elaborate more on this particular case because this money has not helped him over the hurdle at all. He is still in dire need of a further infusion of funds, and the regional director in British Columbia will likely give them to him.

Earlier I said in fairness that the blame must be shared more widely than just by the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and his cabinet colleagues. No matter how hard one tried, it would be difficult to create such a disgraceful situation in only 14 years. But this minister deserves a prize, if for nothing else than the selectivity with which he discharges his trust responsibility and his mandate. He is likely to end up being the minister who will preside over the institutionalization of what I call the lesser of the two evils policy.
This policy started with the white paper in 1969, shortly after the proclamation by the Prime Minister of his just society. In terms of any policy for Indians, justice had to be tempered with equality. That meant, as was pointed out in the white paper of 1969, forced assimilation of the ways of our western civilization. Some people would not see too much wrong with that, but to the Indians and Inuit it would mean nothing less than a cultural transformation. Some use stronger words-cultural and religious genocide.
To appreciate fully what that means, one should compare it with a single language policy, for instance, where suddenly either French or English is no longer an official language and where only one language would be compulsory in school. In fact, anyone who understands anything about the culture and spiritual values of aboriginal people, regardless of where in the world they are found, or anyone who has looked at racial integration from a historical perspective, will know that assimilation or integration is not possible unless some of the most fundamental values of one or the other cultures are sacrificed.
Few of us understand much about the culture of our aboriginal people, but we know that it is inextricably tied to nature and all its creatures. Unlike our western civilization which sees as its Christian-Judeo mission to subdue-the earth and to conquer it, the Indian culture is harmonious with nature, and clearly the two cannot co-exist without very special accommodations. This is in part what I meant when I said earlier that the Indian territories and their people are not represented in the House, of course with one exception-the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar).
In fairness, it should be said that those of our colleagues from all sides of the House who serve on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development not only have a good understanding but also a deep and genuine compassion for the native people they represent. But none of us has walked in a mocassin or can really say what it would be like to accept nature, with all its splendours, with all its generosity but as well its cruelty, as one's spiritual master.
The 1969 policy of forced assimilation, despite consistent denial by the government, is in various stages of implementation even without any constitutional accord which the federal government hopes to get from the provinces in terms of their acquiesence to the forced assimilation strategy. The official land claims policy is an example. The 1980 policy approved by cabinet indicates clearly that settlement means extinguishment of rights and title, that any special rights which may exist are
to be surrendered for cash and/or other considerations such as land, and that the people involved will surrender, to become the wards of the provinces within which the settlement takes place.
The James Bay settlement is the result of this policy, and one of my colleagues will speak specifically about it. Suffice it to say that there is no evidence that any provincial government feels in any way obliged to consider or recognize any special rights our aboriginal people may have, or plans to offer any special services commensurate with such rights.

speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
I have called this the lesser of the two evils policy. The other option which has been considered and tried from time to time is the isolation policy. Despite its abhorrent nature, it is preferred by some native leaders since it at least guarantees some form of cultural and spiritual integrity or sovereignty. In some other countries such an official policy is called apartheid. Although this policy for all intents and purposes existed in Canada, as far as registered Indians are concerned, right up to 1961 when the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker gave them the right to vote in federal elections, all of us surely must agree that this option deserves no further consideration. However, I sometimes wonder whether we would be so sure about it if our country's population consisted of 85 per cent aboriginal people and 15 per cent whites.
This leaves us to consider whether or not there are any other alternatives. Our native people certainly think so, and we in our party certainly agree with them and would like to listen to them. Even though such other options should have been considered and worked out in the context of the first stages of constitutional reform, we think it is not yet too late. However, we also know that any other options which could lead to a solution will not and cannot emerge from the kinds of meetings which were planned in accordance with the constitutional arrangement.
The provincial governments will not, nor should they be expected to, listen or agree to any proposals which would interfere with their own jealously-guarded jurisdictions and ambitions, particularly if any of the proposals include a form of Indian self-government or Indian autonomy. Naturally, we would never condone the development of a governmental structure which would not conform with our federal system. In other words, we do not see a state within a state as a solution.
I am not as certain, however, as the government appears to be, that it would not be possible to grant an Indian government certain powers and jurisdictions which are similar to the powers and jurisdictions enjoyed by the provinces, particularly when it comes to education and culture. Under such an agreement lands, which I have already identified as being lands belonging to the aboriginal people and held in trust for
June 17, 1982

them, and communities on such lands, might be administered under laws similar to municipal acts of the provinces. This idea has been advanced by some native leaders. While it may need a lot of refinement, it may not be too farfetched, particularly when one considers that it was and will be necessary from time to time to give special consideration to any legitimate concerns and aspirations of other ethnocultural groups in society. It is not so farfetched when one considers that all cultures other than that of our native people, of course, and the languages through which they find expression have their origin somewhere else in the world and are from time to time enriched and replenished from their source. As you know, that is true even for the languages and cultures of the so-called two founding races.
The aboriginal people of Canada have no such outside source. Their home has been this continent for at least 16,000 years. The earth of this continent is their soul. To deprive them of an opportunity to protect their language and to move from a firm cultural base to evolve to meet the challenges of tomorrow is nothing less than genocide.
I personally feel that the natives are not yet ready to enter into the discussions that have been arranged to decide their future once and for all. Furthermore, I see it as an example of this government's stubborn, arrogant and inflexible attitude that the native people may be nothing more than observers at the conference.
I have heard evidence to satisfy me that, at least in British Columbia, responsible native political leaders have been starved out and the department has purchased itself the kind of help from among the Indians who may be prepared to sell out their brothers and sisters for their own selfish gain. They will no doubt be the representatives at the conference. I referred to one such person earlier. If they are the kind of people being groomed to represent the native interests at the conferences, native interests will be doomed for sure.
These are harsh words but I stand by them. Why do you think that the committee unanimously approved the report, including all the Liberal members who served? Regardless of what the minister says about using trickery to achieve a report, they were all there. We spent three weeks writing this report and the words in the report are strong. Why do hon. members think all the members on that committee unanimously approved that report-and agreed that it should be tabled in the House-expressing dismay and condemnation over the way the minister and his regional czars are discharging their trust responsibility?
My colleagues and I will insist that some specific problems which are more like Mafia-type operations-I will not withdraw that word as well-will be redressed without delay. We do not intend to let these matters rest for another year. We will insist that the fifth annual report of the Indian affairs committee be implemented. We will insist on that because the conditions which exist as a result of this government's policies

toward our native people are a disgrace and a shame which all Canadians must share.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Chenier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to express my disappointment and concern with the language of the notice of motion which is now before the House. I would also like to express my disappointment and concern with the language which was used by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) about both the department and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). I believe that some of the inaccuracies which he expressed in his speech today were very well explained to him, but he preferred (o use the same tactics that he used in the committee to try to impress upon the Canadian people that we have problems.
The government has long recognized that there are very major outstanding questions, problems and challenges that have to be faced with respect to Canada's aboriginal people. The complexity of these matters is well known to hon. members on both sides of the House. Solutions which governments and aboriginal people seek are not easily attained. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), when he was Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, realized that. In private conversations he has admitted that it is difficult to obtain a consensus.
From the government's perspective, searching for those solutions involves a delicate balance. On the one hand, we need to respond to the need and aspirations of Canada's aboriginal people. On the other hand, we must meet our special obligations and responsibilities as a government in a manner which respects accountability to Parliament for the expenditure of public funds.
Not only are these issues complex in themselves, but the political environment in which governments and aboriginal people must search for solutions is rapidly evolving and is not without its difficulties.
As consitutional discussions have proceeded in recent years, Canada's aboriginal people have articulated more specific views on their present and future place within Canadian society. In some areas the positions presented are extremely difficult to accommodate under Canadian political sturctures and systems. In other areas, aspirations are realizable if government at all levels and Canada's aboriginal peoples can work effectively together.
It is this sense of complexity and challenge that is not reflected in the motion now before us. It is my belief that this government has demonstrated a priority commitment to improving the social and economic conditions of Canada's aboriginal people While it is not possible to move in all major new directions at once, as members on the other side of the House discovered while they were in government, I believe that not only is the commitment of this government apparent but so, too, are the results.
Over the course of the last decade major changes in developing land claims policies and attempting to resolve claims have

occurred. Major advances in key program areas such as education, housing, economic development, support of Indian culture and language have also occurred. We have increased government expenditures in all program areas and have done this at a time of fiscal restraint.
The government does recognize that major problems remain outstanding and while the ability to move quickly, particularly in a period of fiscal restraint, is not as great as one would like, the commitment to resolving these issues is demonstrated.
I would like to now focus in more detail on the accomplishments which I believe reflect our commitment on the part of our government. Consider for a moment some of the positive achievements of the last couple of years in programs which deal directly with the priority concerns of native people These achievements demonstrate that in meeting its obligation and commitment to native people the government is making considerable progress.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
The government is committed to pursue the Phase II conference with determination and good faith. As a matter of fact, the first meeting between the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the three national associations of Canada will take place next Tuesday. This does not mean that we will reach agreement on all issues, but it does mean that we will reach an understanding of native positions. It also means that we will have honest discussions and a clarification of the issues. It does mean that we will make a real effort to reach agreement.
At the Phase II meetings, delegates of native peoples will be seated at the table. They will sit down next to the Prime Minister and the first ministers of the provinces. The agenda will include, to quote Part IV of the Canada Act, "an item respecting constitutional matters that directly affect the aboriginal peoples of Canada, including the identification and definition of those peoples to be included in the Constitution of Canada". Let me add that the native leadership commands the respect of all of us for keeping native rights front and centre over the past months.
I would like to suggest that the Canada Act will become a powerful instrument that will help the Indian, Inuit and Metis people achieve their goals in Canadian society. On the one hand, it recognizes aboriginal and treaty rights and thus protects Indian and Inuit identity. On the other hand, it
guarantees the rights and freedoms of native people as citizens of Canada.
Second, we are making progress in co-operation with the native people toward eliminating discrimination among men and women in native communities. More than a year ago, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development made it possible for bands to exempt themselves from certain provisions of the Indian Act, namely those which cause women to lose their status if they marry white men and those which cause children to lose their status. At last count, 48 bands had requested the exemption from the discriminatory provisions affecting women and about 270 others asked to be exempted from the double mother clause which affects children's rights. We expect that additional bands will avail themselves of this option in coming months. The government has also clearly indicated its commitment to removing the present discriminatory provisions of the Indian Act following consultations with Canada's aboriginal people.
Third, we are making progress in assisting native communities to strengthen their system of band government. In discussions with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development over the last couple of years, the Indian leadership has expressed the need for establishing self-government at the band level and taking charge of their own financial affairs. They want to transfer to their administration more of the development and delivery of programs.
The minister has supported the native peoples in this objective. In fact, we have been successful in transferring control and the delivery of various programs to Indian bands. By the end of last year, for example, 385 bands across Canada were administering social assistance programs on reserves. In British Columbia, 60 per cent of the regional budget is now administered by Indian organizations. It is the other 40 per cent which is administered by the regional office that did not appear in the figures that were cited by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River and that made the figures appear so abominable.
We are looking at ways and means of strengthening Indian band government in order to enable us to deal more effectively with Indian demands for increased autonomy and still provide a basis for greater social and economic development. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is examining a variety of proposals, including proposals which would enable bands to move out from under the more restrictive provisions of the Indian Act in certain circumstances. Any proposals, of course, will be the subject of consultations with Indian people, and these are going on already.
[ Translation]
Now, a few words about education. Since 1980, native people have made tremendous progress towards achieving control of their education system. This is true of both the Inuit and the Indian people. Today, there are three Indian and Inuit schoolboards at the provincial level. Two were created following the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. In nine
June 17, 1982

provinces and in the two territories, 58 cultural centres are now being managed by Indians and Inuit. School enrolment in Indian communities has made considerable progress at all levels. There are now 157 schools serving 10,000 students, and it is expected that enrolment will increase to 20,000 by 1986. The most impressive gains have been made in post-secondary education, both in the vocational sector and the post-secondary programs. In 1969, for instance, 800 Indians were enrolled in post-secondary programs, while by the end of last year, their number had increased to 6,000.
I shall now mention some of our achievements in the field of economic development. Considering our objective to have certain areas of federal jurisdiction revert to native peoples, we have stressed community-based rather than large-scale development projects, with a view to responding to the desire for increased autonomy expressed by native peoples. Among these projects, to name only a few, I would mention the wild rice project in Ontario and the caribou management program in northern Saskatchewan, northern Manitoba and the Northwest Territories which was finalized about two weeks ago.
We have started creating jobs at the community and reserve levels, but much remains to be done. For instance, the department's Ontario regional office provides counselling for Indian businessmen and local projects, a program that has helped to stimulate job creation and to safeguard existing jobs. In last November's budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) mentioned additional funds totalling several million dollars which will be used for economic development in native communities. These funds are in addition to funds already allocated. Last year, for instance, we set aside $8 million to ensure that we would not have to turn down valid economic development projects because of lack of funds. Once again, these are supplementary funds. In addition, $5 million was earmarked to help Indians take advantage of the opportunities offered by large resource developments. In a period of budgetary restraint, I think the House will agree that the amounts involved are impressive. These figures and the new approaches involved clearly demonstrate that the government is prepared to meet its commitment to improve the economic and social status of native peoples.
The Norman Wells project should illustrate the truth of this statement to everyone's satisfaction. In this particular development, our concern is both with protecting the environment and protecting the future of native communities. We have insisted that the entire population, and especially native people, be able to obtain jobs and participate in the project on a partnership basis. Over $20 million have been spent on these programs which include providing technical and general training to help native people find jobs, either in the oil fields or on pipeline construction sites. As work progresses, at least 240 jobs and business opportunities estimated at more than $100 million will be made available to the local population. In addition, native people associations will be able to take part in joint
Supply
ventures. With the skills and experience acquired as workers or entrepreneurs, native people will be able to start similar projects.
The two-year waiting period set for Norman Wells can and must be used to good advantage. During this period, we shall be able to establish training programs and give Indians and other people a chance to prepare for future opportunities for employment and subcontracting. Thus, the communities involved will have ample time to adjust to the situation.
The House will be pleased to know that the project has been enthusiastically received by the Indian people, the territorial government and business groups.

In consultation with Indian bands, we are progressing in establishing joint ventures in major capital projects such as schools, health clinics, band administration buildings and so on. Such ventures will enable band councils to be rightly involved in all aspects of a capital project on their reserve, from the design of a construction to the actual day-by-day operations. Furthermore, the joint venture guidelines that we are developing will also guarantee jobs, training opportunities and related economic developments at the band level.
Over the last two years the minister has met with native people and their leaders in all the regions of Canada on land claims. I believe that the actions that the minister and the department have taken reflect the concerns of native people with respect to claims. The vast majority of Canadians, I believe, would agree that the land claims have been left unresolved for too long. We are responding to that view in a positive way.
I hope that in Manitoba, for instance, where I am involved in land claims, the new provincial government will not have the attitude of the previous Progressive Conservative government that was not interested even in beginning negotiations on land claims.

conclusion, and we have allocated funds to support native organizations in their research, preparation and negotiations.
Recently the minister participated, along with the Hon. Allan Williams, the attorney general of British Columbia, in the signing of an accord with the Penticton band. Under this agreement, the band will receive $14 million and the return of some 12,000 acres of land that was severed from their reserve in 1916. This agreement should be regarded as a milestone-
It took 70 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Sure it took us 70 years, but we did it. What did the opposition do when it was in government? How many claims were resolved? None. Six months?
You did one in 60 years, for one band.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
In addition, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) recently participated in the signing of an agreement with the Wagmatcook band for loss of reserve lands dating back to confederation. Once again the government is clearly demonstrating its determination to deal fairly and to settle long-standing grievances. This commitment is based on policies on specific and comprehensive claims which have been reconfirmed and inscribed in two recent DIAND publications, "In All Fairness" and "Outstanding Business".
Just two months ago the minister, together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), jointly announced a new program for fighting native alcohol and drug abuse. It was backed by a commitment of $154 million. This will be a permanently funded program to support native peoples in their efforts to prevent and treat these problems in their own communities. The successful implementation of the program will depend on the development of community-based projects which they will initiate and administer. Nearly all reserves will be involved in the program; the number of treatment centres will increase from eight, under the present program, to 30, and the number of in-patient beds will increase from 140 to 730. It will be operated with the assistance of 800 trained native therapists and helpers.
In February I participated on behalf of the minister, along with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), is signing the Canada-Manitoba Indian child welfare agreement. The Indian signatory was the Four Nations Confederacy. The agreement is a major advance in devolving responsibility in the Field of child welfare to the native communities. This agreement will create 53 permanent jobs at the reserve level and will cost $14 million over a five-year period. This landmark agreement, the very first in Canada, delegates
powers to Indian child care authorities and band governments in Manitoba who now have the resources to deal with this new responsibility.
These are some of the achievements, Mr. Speaker, of the last year or two to which all Canadians can point with pride. They are the result of the determination on the part of the federal government to deal with Indian communities in a fair and equitable manner, and to assist Indians, individually and as communities, to achieve self-reliance. They are equally the result of the determination on the part of native people to control their own destiny.
It is with this type of progress that the government has demonstrated, and continues to demonstrate, its will and support to working co-operatively with the aboriginal peoples of Canada. Together we can and will effect major changes and resolve outstanding problems. Not only is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development specifically, and the government, doing their utmost to discharge their obligations and responsibilities, but in many areas federal programs and approaches go significantly further than those required as a matter of legal responsibility and obligation.
It is also because of this progress that I view with real disappointment the wording of the motion before the House. There is no doubt that much remains to be done. For further progress to be made, the co-operation of all members of this House-individually and through established vehicles such as the standing committee, as well as other levels of government working co-operatively with Canada's aboriginal peoples-is required. I call on all members to demonstrate their cooperation and I especially would like to see some members of the official opposition, rather than trying to obstruct, trying to offer real co-operation, so that we can resolve these problems as fast as we can.
