June 17, 1982

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Schellenberger:
That this House condemns the government, and in particular, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, for its failure to meet any of the objectives for which the government continues to seek authority to spend in excess of one billion dollars in this fiscal year on behalf of Canada's aboriginal peoples, for its tolerance of the miserable conditions existing in native communities throughout Canada which are of a standard vastly inferior to those found in most Third World countries, for the minister's failure to exercise his obligatory trust responsibility, and for the minister's contempt of Parliament as manifested by his deliberate refusal to comply with the statutory obligations which legally require him to report to the House on the progress of the implementation of the James Bay agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this important topic of the wellbeing of the Indian people of Canada and also to look at some of the conduct of the Department of Indian affairs.
This topic is important perhaps for two basic and fundamental reasons. First of all, our government is spending over $1 billion supposedly for the wellbeing of the Indian people of Canada. I believe that neither the Canadian people in general nor the Indian people in particular are getting their money's worth for that $1 billion. We spend $1 billion to perpetuate an inflated bureaucracy in the Department of Indian Affairs and the depressed and depressing economy of poverty and despair in most Indian communities. As the watchdog over the public treasury, this House must be concerned.
Second, this topic is important, Mr. Speaker, for perhaps a more basic and fundamental reason, but a reason which it is harder to define. It concerns who we are as a people and how we see ourselves as a people. Perhaps it would help us at this time if we contrast our vision of Canada with the way in which one writer saw Argentina over the last decade. V. S. Naipaul, in "The Return of Eva Peron", writes of "A simple history of Indian genocide and European take-over". The author says:
There is as yet in Argentina no myth of the noble Indian. The memory of the genocide is too close; it is still something to be dismissed in a line or two in the annals. In Argentina, the detestation of the vanished Pampa Indian is instinctive and total. The Argentine terror is that people in other countries might think of Argentina as an Indian country-
Land in Argentina ... is still only a commodity. It is an investment, a hedge against inflation. It can be alienated without heartache.
I believe that Canadians want a different relationship with the Indian people and with the land from what Naipaul saw in Argentina. Perhaps some people over-romanticize it, but the fact is that Indian, Inuit and Metis people do have a close relationship with the land. It is a relationship others of us have lost but still recognize as important. On this basis we see that aboriginal people and their wellbeing are of vital importance to the Canadian psyche.
Supply
In Canada, from at least the time of the Royal proclamation of George III, we have always recognized that Indian people had a special and unique status. However inadequately we recognize this status both in the BNA Act and in the recently proclaimed Canada Act, it is there. Often the government of the day has been uncomfortable with special status and has sought to eliminate it by some program of assimilation. The Indian people have suffered under the treatment they have received, but they have stubbornly refused to be assimilated into a non-Indian society. They see remaining Indian as being something very basic to their lives. They have held to some vision of themselves as a separate and unique people who have a special role and a special place in our world.
We have neglected the Indian people. We have seen them die of European diseases. We have alienated their children from their parents, their communities, their language and their culture. We have tried to destroy traditional Indian religions and their political institutions. We have subjected them to alien laws in a colonial-type bureaucracy. Although some of our policies may have been genocidal in their results, we have always maintained that we have worked for the best interests of the Indian people. Perhaps we did but, strangely enough, in the process we ended up with most of the Indian land! In the process of working for what we said were the best interests of the Indian people, we destroyed the base of the Indian economy and left the Indians dependent on our generosity-our welfare payments.
The way we allow Indian people to live says a great deal about what kind of people we are. At present when our economy is in such a shambles some people might be tempted to deny or ignore the needs of Indians because we have many other problems in Canada. Nearly two million people are unemployed. There are no jobs for the young people coming out of our high schools this week and next week. The value of our dollar is sinking, interest rates are rising and there is a growing number of bankruptcies.
With these difficulties it might be easy to forget about such issues as aboriginal and treaty rights, land claims, decent housing, water and sewage on reserves, economic development for Indian people or ending discrimination against Indian women. However, there are two reasons why we cannot do that. First, we have a debt of honour to the Indian people. I do not believe we will want to say to them that we have gone morally bankrupt. We have a debt of honour, and I believe we must meet it. Second, it is important that we recognize that Indian people themselves are part of the total Canadian economy, and if we give them the means for economic development in their own communities and if we make available to them proper funds for housing and infrastructure, this money will circulate in the Canadian economy and help all of us. What we cannot afford is to perpetuate a welfare economy, so I emphasize the importance of this debate this afternoon.
In our Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development there is usually a relatively non-partisan spirit,
18566

June 17, 1982
Supply
and 1 must say I was pleased and impressed when the government members of that committee agreed to the fifth report. On the other hand, I cannot see how government members could have opposed it in good conscience, after they and the rest of us heard the testimony of Indian people from across the country about the conditions they face. In a non-partisan way the fifth report says exactly the same thing as this motion does with perhaps more loaded language. I look forward to the participation of other government members in today's debate because the fifth report of the standing committee, which was accepted by the House, has a real message for the minister and for the cabinet from all members of that committee, Liberals, Conservatives and New Democrats alike. We hope the minister will hear that message and act on it.
There are three basic issues with which we need to deal this afternoon. First, there is a need for Indian people to be involved in the budgetary process. Second, there is a need for greater funding for the Indian people. Third, there is a need for dismantling the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Let us look at these in order.
First, the Indian people must be involved in the budgetary process. It is a very frustrating experience for Indian bands to have to be accountable to the department but to have no participation in saying how funds are to be allocated. It is a very frustrating experience when a band such as the Cowichan band is not able to get any indication of what the target figures for its budget will be and then, in the middle of March, to be told that because their budget will exceed $3 million and because of changing Treasury Board requirements, they will now have to submit a Treasury Board application before their budget can be approved. They are told this about two weeks before the end of the fiscal year. It is a very frustrating experience for people such as the Oweekano band, who have expressed their concerns in a letter as follows:
Our initial comments regarding this morning's meeting are not complimentary to say the least. We must voice our dissatisfaction with your process of negotiations where we are required to merely jot down those allocations you have decided we should get. We came away from the meeting thoroughly frustrated with the way in which small and isolated Bands are dealt with including ours.
Large bands are told two weeks before the deadline that they have to submit Treasury Board applications for their budgets. Small bands are called in, the so-called process of consultation involves having them jot down which items are approved, and that is that.
Then there is the problem that even after a budget has been approved and even when Indian bands are punctual in getting their quarterly reports in, the department is very lax in getting moneys out. Our committee heard testimony from the Nes-kainlith band in British Columbia that because of delays in the payment of funds which were included in the budget, that band has had to pay something like $10,000 to $12,000 a year in interest.
We are hearing some rather despairing cries from the banks these days about their profits, but I do not think it is really in the interests of the Canadian people that the department should be so slow in making payments to Indian bands that they are having to pay interest in order to maintain some line of credit at the banks. It is absolutely essential that the Indian
people be involved in the budgetary process from the very beginning and not simply be called in at the end and told what there might be.
Second, I would like to speak about the lack of funds for identified needs. One of the reasons for the present crisis in funding is probably due to the success of one of the programs of the government. Over the last several years the government has adopted a policy of devolving administrative responsibility to the Indian people, and during that time the leaders of the Indian people have developed considerable expertise in identifying the needs of their people. It is no longer a matter of their simply accepting what the Indian agents give them. They have developed an expertise in identifying their needs but they find that the money to take care of those needs is not available.
We used to expect Indian people to get by in poverty after we had taken away the base of their economy. Today we are making promises and we expect them to get by on those, even when they are not kept. I should like to put a few examples on the record, Mr. Speaker.
A few years ago Indian students were given a spending allowance of $10 per week. In spite of the fact that inflation has cut away at the dollar and that everyone else is getting more money, Indian students are still expected to get by on that amount of spending money. Sometimes it makes the difference between whether they are able to attend school away from home or not. It we are concerned about Indian education-and we all claim to be-then we should ensure that students receive enough spending money.
I was pleased to hear the minister say in the House yesterday that he is engaged in the process of revising upwards the standards for Indian schools. Ten years ago standards were set for Indian schools but then the department decided that they were too high and reduced them. In most provinces today the federal standard for Indian schools is below that of the provinces. I was pleased to hear that the minister is going to take action on that matter and will watch closely to see what is done about it.
A program called the infant stimulation program was shared by five bands on Vancouver Island. Initially this program received funding for the training of young Indian people so that they could work with parents and pre-school children. For three years it received funds from the community development program on a declining basis and no other federal department has taken up the slack. This was a very good program and now it is threatened because of lack of funds.
The Union of New Brunswick Indians has brought to our attention many times its concern about the termination of the community development hot lunch program for children. This is not limited to Indian children. When there is a lack of money in the home children are often sent to school hungry. The hot lunch program was an attempt to provide basic nutrition for them because it is recognized that children cannot learn on an empty stomach. Money for the hot lunch program did not come through, however.
June 17, 1982

In Mission, British Columbia, the residential school of St. Mary's is facing budget cuts. This will mean a decrease of ten in the number of staff and of 35 in the number of students. Many of these students come from broken homes or isolated communities or communities where there is not adequate housing. This residence should be maintained until there is something to take its place.
Recreation budgets have not been maintained. That might seem to be a small thing to a departmental official but for the Indian people recreation and sports are one way in which they can develop a sense of confidence and pride in themselves. The budget for these items should not be cut at this time.
On many occasions the government has announced that $345 million is available for economic development over the next few years. That money has been promised but so far we have not seen any of it. No mechanism has been developed in consultation with the Indian people to allocate the money to the Indian, Metis and Inuit people.
When we visit Indian villages we see how the people suffer because their housing lacks adequate sewer and water facilities. I visited the Penelakut village in my own constituency and there I saw plastic pipes bringing the water supply up to the porch of a house. That was the extent of the running water. Side by side with the water pipes were other plastic pipes for the disposal of sewage. Both pipes were leaking, Mr. Speaker. This is the kind of situation that prevails in those communities. It is very depressing for someone from the outside but for the people of the village it is life threatening. In many Indian villages the people live on the verge of serious epidemics. We have heard testimony about this from the Cree of James Bay. We have to take action, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to make a few short comments about the work of the department. The employees are demoralized. They are not bad people, Mr. Speaker, but the system is wrong. The Indian people want the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to get off their backs.
The government should immediately begin the process of involving the Indian people in the budgetary process from the beginning. An acceptable method must be found for the aboriginal peoples to have control over the $70 million economic development fund-which is eventually supposed to total $345 million.
The fifth report of the committee asked that a special capital fund be set up for the infrastructure for housing, sewage and water supplies. We ask that the report on the implementation of the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement be tabled immediately and that the Tait report on this agreement be tabled and funds provided. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I urge that supplementary estimates be provided to meet the needs of the Indian people and that action be taken to decrease the size of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak in this debate on an opposition motion. The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Supply
Oberle) who opened the debate referred to the surprise that some people might feel at having a debate on this subject today. I believe he referred to the fact that the subject is close to the heart of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), that is, involvement in the North-South dialogue. I agree with the hon. member because I too have that feeling.
One of the reasons I have enjoyed my work on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development is that I happen to be one of the few members of that committee whose riding does not have an Indian band. There are several all around my riding, however. As a matter of fact, a number of Indian young people attend one of the secondary schools in London West.
I want to talk about some of the advances in education which have taken place for Indian students as a direct result of government involvement over the years. Already it has been stated that there is a non-partisan feeling on the part of the standing committee when we meet, and 1 would agree with that. That is why I was rather discouraged and disheartened when I heard some of the words expressed earlier by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River. That certainly was not the feeling expressed during many of the hearings. As a matter of fact, I had the feeling when we met with many Indian bands and band councils over many weeks that while many problems do exist there is a respect held for the current Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) by many of those groups and there is a definite spirit of co-operation between the native peoples and the minister. I think that has to be said and underlined because it came through very loud and clear in many of our hearings.
I would like to take one objection to references by the previous speaker to the fifth report of the standing committee as coinciding fully with the opposition motion. I reject that observation. While there certainly are areas of criticism in the fifth report, it does not coincide with the entire wording of the motion up for debate today. I seems clear that the motion, when it speaks of the government failing to meet any of its objectives in respect of programs designed to afford development of Indian people in this country, overlooks some very obvious steps which have been taken-and I stress this-in concert with the Indian peoples themselves. This is particularly true in the matter of Indian education. As I earlier mentioned, many of the Indian young people in southwestern Ontario come into my riding for education, and that is why I want to comment on this area this afternoon.
In addressing this topic, I believe it would be useful, Mr. Speaker, to outline the relationship of changes in specific educational programs to the fundamental changes we have seen coming to fruition in the last decade of Indian education in this country. If we go back to the early days of Indian education, we see that from about 1850 schooling for Canadian Indian children was segregated in order to be protective. This derived from the government's view of the social climates

June 17, 1982
Supply
of the growing immigrant communities as being potentially injurious to the welfare of Indian groups. The dark side of this residential schooling for Indian children has been well documented; the enforced separation of children from families and devaluing of the Indian culture and languages involved. The large majority of Indian children, in the years from confederation to about 1950, were educated in residential schools on reserve lands. During this period, however, a small but significant number of Indian people were able to achieve high academic levels.
Following World War II, raised public consciousness of human rights and race relations as well as representations from Indian people caused a change in education policy. During the 1960s, following some consideration of the condition of native minority groups and at the urging of some Indian leaders, the federal government moved towards encouraging the participation of Indian youth in provincial education systems. As part of that movement, the government introduced special programs designed to support financially the integration of Indian students in provincial schools. These included school supplies, travel, personal and other miscellaneous allowances. The government was addressing directly the priorities of Indian school development as they were perceived at that time.
As many hon. members are aware, however, Mr. Speaker, the work of the standing committee and the National Indian Brotherhood brought about a changed government posture which, in 1973, acknowledged that Indian education, like that provided for their fellow citizens, should defer to the principles of local control and parental responsibility. Indian control is not, of course, restricted to band-administered schools. Even within provincial jurisdictions where Indian control is admittedly more difficult to achieve, mechanisms for enabling greater involvement of Indian people in education are being developed.
In the last decade, reflecting the social advances of Indian people generally, we have seen some significant trends in Indian education as communities have asserted their influence on administration, curriculum content, teacher training and other critical segments of the system. The impact of both Indian and the department's initiatives has also been felt within provincial jurisdictions with provincial departments of education moving towards greater recognition of native Canadian cultural realities in schooling generally.
An important indicator of the place of Indian cultures in Canadian curricula is the fact that over 32,000 out of over
73,000	Indian students study native languages in federal, provincial and band-operated schools. Significant progress has been made in increasing Indian involvement in all aspects of eduction. In 1970, about 200 Indian school committees had some, generally minor, responsibility for education programming. However, by 1980 three Indian or Inuit school boards had been created under provincial law: the Nishgas of B.C. and the Cree and Kativik school boards of northern Quebec; 450 of the 573 bands are administering all or parts of their programs. There are also 137 band-operated on-reserve schools. There are band-administered education budgets.
including post-secondary and student residences. These have grown to almost $110 million from about $7 million in the early 1970s. The percentage of Indian administrators and teachers in federal schools has grown to 30 per cent.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that policy and programming changes and, most importantly, the increased decision-making role of Indian authorities have necessitated the addition or elimination of various programs as priorities change with changing circumstances. Local control has naturally resulted in greater attention being focused on the resources required to continue to improve the quality of on-reserve educational services. Inevitably, reallocation of budgets based on departmental and band education authority reviews of priorities lead to decreases in, or the discontinuation of, certain discretionary programs. I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is realistic to allude to this management process of redefining priorities and reallocating available resources as "cutbacks" if at the same time we are increasing our over-all expenditures on the education operations and maintenance budget, which in 1980-81 amounted to over $278 million.
It should be noted, as well, Mr. Speaker, that the department is limited by the Indian Act in responding to requests for educational services to Indian elementary and secondary students. While the federal government affirms its special relationship with Indian people, it is clear that those residing off reserves are fully entitled to all those services available to other provincial citizens, since both groups have the same obligations to their provincial administrations in terms of contributing as taxpayers.
Let me briefly address the question of how tuition agreements relate to the principle of Indian control. This is of primary concern, especially in light of the fact that in 1980-81 about 53 per cent of Indian elementary and secondary school students resident on reserves or Crown lands attended schools under provincial jurisdiction. In the same year, band education authorities controlled 26 per cent of the tuition fees paid to provincial agencies. It has been projected that in 1981-82 over
41,000	reserve or Crown land residents attended provincial schools at a total cost, excluding capital, of $145.1 million.
The jurisdictional situation makes the negotiating and administration of tuition agreements quite complex. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development operates within a context influenced by Indian government, the minister's responsibilities under the Indian Act and the constitutional powers assigned to the provinces. The reality of provincial jurisdiction has necessitated differing approaches to the development of tuition agreements, with the most important variable being the extent to which Indian education authorities participate in the process. This varies from Indian operation of provincial school boards to parents having only the status of visitors in schools.
Where Indian people have opted to make use of provincial educational services, the department sees a primary responsibility of the provincial authority as being the encouragement
June 17, 1982

of Indian involvement in the design, delivery, administration, control, review and evaluation of provincial education programs. In such situations the role of band education authorities is considered to include representing the interest of Indian parents and communities; negotiating federal and provincial service agreements; managing education budgets; accounting for results to parents and the community generally.
The department sees its present role in this matter as being twofold. First, there will be continuing emphasis on co-operating with regional Indian associations and bands in seeking the enactment of provincial legislation to increase Indian representation on education decision-making bodies. Second, at the local level, department staff will continue to support Indian initiatives which aim at achieving more meaningful participation of Indian parents in determining the nature of programming in provincial schools.
At the same time, as I mentioned a few moments ago, there have been significant advances in the post-secondary education program for Indians and Inuit which has been specifically developed by the department. During the 1970s, as education and particularly post-secondary education became for Indians the single most important means of improving their standard of living and providing opportunity for intellectual, social and cultural development, departmental programs were evolved and developed to give full measure to those aspirations. Greater access to post-secondary education resulted in a near 100 per cent graduate employment, a teaching staff for Indian schools which is almost 30 per cent Indian, significant increases in the numbers of Indian lawyers, social workers, nurses, administrators and managers.
The Indian graduates have assumed lead roles in the development of band government and Indian politics. It was our opportunity as members of the standing committee to meet many of these individuals as they presented themselves on behalf of the various bands and councils throughout this country. Indian graduates have become models to inspire younger generations and they symbolize the turn-around from drop-out schooling to a contemporary student retrieval thrust spearheaded by active Indian educational leadership. Indian educators in curriculum development work and through cultural education centres have revitalized Indian languages and culture so that Indian people now have the opportunity to regain the pride in their Indian identity. These factors have led to a very rapidly expanding program in terms of enrolments, graduations, and expenditures.
For example, the post-secondary education of Indians has been the prime force in the establishment of the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College of the University of Regina, the Blue Quills post-secondary centre of Alberta and the establishment of university native studies programs in every province, the beginning of an Indian business management training network, and other initiatives, all of which point to the Canadian Indian community being poised for a new and prosperous era in the twenty first century.
Almost ten years ago, Mr. Speaker, the then minister of Indian affairs, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), in addressing the council of ministers of education, spoke of
Supply
the joint obligation of the provinces and the federal government to respond to the need to improve Indian education by ensuring parental involvement, developing appropriate curricula, expanding teacher training requirements and encouraging Indians to enter the profession as well as meeting the demand for teacher aids.
We have today good solid indicators in the federal, provincial and band-controlled education systems that these ideas have been and continue to be valued and respected. The federal government's role has changed visibly over these years as the Indian people have assumed more of their rightful role in educating their children. Recognizing the role formal education plays in cultural continuity, the federal government will continue to support the Indian people in their efforts to achieve their goals in this most fundamental aspect of human endeavour. I think it was as late as yesterday, in answer to a question from a member of the New Democratic Party, that the Minister of Indian Affairs referred to a particular situation dealing with the building of a school where he gave his support to this matter.
I want to reiterate in closing that this federal government will continue to support the Indian people in all aspects of education so that they may develop their own wherewithal in achieving their goals in this most fundamental aspect of human endeavour.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that in trying times those already in difficulty get hit the hardest. As this recession deepens it is evident that many of our native people are suffering more than usual. My colleague, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), has, I think, laid out very clearly the foundation to what is happening to the Indian community or, more importantly, what is not happening to our native people.
The inaction of this government, the false promises of the minister, and the inertia and callousness of a huge and insensitive bureaucracy, are grinding many of Canada's native people into the dust. The Third World conditions endured by native people across this land are well documented by groups who come before hearings of the standing committee. Unbelievable and disgraceful stories of pain, suffering and betrayal often unfold before us. By and large, Canadians are unaware of these conditions, but any member of the standing committee who has listened day in and day out, month after month and year after year, is well aware of these terrible situations. How any government can go on year after year and not get to the root of the problems and solve them is beyond comprehension.
What is interesting to me is that we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who travels the world advising Third World countries on how to deal with their problems, while in our own country, and in his own province of Quebec, conditions exist that are on a par with any in the Third World.
Let me give a very recent example of some things that have just happened in Quebec. I refer to a report in the Montreal Gazette for June 12, 1982. The first part of the story deals

June 17, 1982
Supply
with a young Indian couple with a one-month old baby. They took the sick child to see a nurse in a nearby community. The nurse gave the baby a very cursory examination and told the couple to take the child home. That night the baby died. This young couple went to bury the baby on the reserve. As they were doing this, provincial police landed in a helicopter. They took the baby away and told this couple that they were not allowed to bury the child because there was no death certificate. A month later the police returned the child in a carnation milk carton to the parents. There was no explanation whatsoever about what had happened.
And this is Canada in 1982.

I shall quote one sentence from the newspaper article in the Montreal Gazette. It reads:
It's commonplace, Savard says, for the bodies of Indian children to be returned to their parents in pieces, in green plastic garbage bags or in boxes.
That is Canada, that is Quebec, in 1982. We have 74 members sitting across from us who come from Quebec, yet some of the worst horror stories which were told before the standing committee came out of that province. I cannot understand the Prime Minister letting these kinds of things happen in his own province. I talked with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) about this particular situation, and she assured me that it was true. Also she assured me that she would investigate it and do her best to ensure that it did not happen again. These were the kinds of situations about which we heard time and time again. It is just completely unacceptable.
An important part of the motion before us today deals with the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement. The last part of the motion reads:
-and for the minister's contempt of Parliament as manifested by his deliberate refusal to comply with the statutory obligations which legally require him to report to the House on the progress of the implementation of the James Bay agreement.
Before getting into the James Bay agreement in detail and that particular problem, let me explain how the agreement came about and what it entailed. It was signed on November 11, 1975. It is a 454-page agreement full of promises to the Indian and Inuit people of northern Quebec. It is a contract signed by two governments, the Government of Quebec and the Government of Canada. Also it was signed by the Cree and Inuit people of northern Quebec. It promised that, in exchange for about half the land mass of Quebec and for $225 million over a period of 20 years, the Indians and the Inuit would give up their aboriginal title to a land mass which was their home for centuries and centuries. In return for this, aside from the cash settlement of which they only receive a bit every year, they were promised improved government services, the allotment of 5,000 square miles of land, limited autonomy for the Cree and Inuit, and many other specific things. For instance, they were promised improved health care, better housing, community infrastructures such as sewer and water, air strips, improved educational facilities, roads, fire protection and many more things. They were also promised, because they were so far behind and in such bad shape, that there would be
a catch-up and a continuation of the programs received by native people across the country. For all this they gave up their aboriginal title. Five years later, by August, 1980, it was a certainty that the agreement was not working.
The Cree and Inuit people appeared before the standing committee in the spring of 1981 with a litany of financial and social complaints, such as the death of children. Situations were documented by very respected doctors from the Montreal General Hospital. One such report was given to us by Dr. Gary Pekeles, a highly respected pediatrician at the Montreal General Hospital. I should like to quote a few lines from his report on April 16, 1981:
The purpose of this report is to describe an epidemic of infantile gastroenteritis among the native population of the Hudson Bay and James Bay regions of Quebec that occurred in the spring and summer of 1980. This disease affected many children under two years in the villages in this region. In several villages a majority of such children became ill. At least 80 children were hospitalized because of it, many with long and complicated courses; almost half required transfer to children's hospitals in Montreal. At least seven children died with gastroenteritis. This occurred in a region that certainly has less than 1,000 children under two years old.
We heard testimony from one community at Rupert House where the raw sewage from the local medical clinic was being discharged upstream from the native people's water supply. This community experienced an outbreak of gastroenteritis among its population. It was just an endless cycle-the children went to hospital, sewage was discharged in the river above the water intake, and around and around it went. We were told in committee that this would be looked after by a representative of the Quebec department of health and welfare. Several months later when the minister visited the community to look at the situation, he found, much to his dismay and to our disgust, that it had not been dealt with. It has been dealt with since. That is the type of story we heard in the committee hearings.
During all these health problems which the Cree and Inuit were having, the federal Department of National Health and Welfare decided to pull out of the area, to take out all its health support services because it misread the act. What was supposed to happen is that when the Cree and Inuit were ready to take over their health services, the federal government was to withdraw. But reading between the lines of the agreement, it withdrew and left the native people high and dry.
What has this led to? Since the Indian people have not received any help in the area of health, they have been required to spend money that was to go into such things as economic development on health, welfare, sewage and water systems which were supposed to be provided by the Government of Canada and the Government of Quebec. It was well summed up in testimony before the committee by Grand Chief Billy Diamond, when he stated:
It is true that the Crees have received compensation moneys. However, these compensation moneys were in partial exchange for their aboriginal rights and were to be used as basic heritage funds for future generations of the Cree people. This was unquestionably recognized by both the governments and the Crees during the negotiations and at the time of signing of the agreement. What has
June 17, 1982

instead resulted is that the Crees, because of the critical health and sanitation problems and dramatic absence of accommodation and infrastructures in the Cree communities, have been forced to spend over one-quarter of their compensation revenues on housing and infrastructure.
The committee, on hearing this, was so outraged that it did something it had never done before. It drafted a report which was attached to the estimates report tabled in the House. It asked the minister to take immediate action. The action which the minister took was to appoint a commissioner to go up there to look over the entire situation. He was to return with a report and recommendations which would go before cabinet. Last fall he returned with an 87-page report which documented most of the situations in the area. Some time in January the report was put before cabinet, but we are still awaiting a decision.
Approximately 11,000 people in the area have been waiting since 1975 for justice. A safeguard in the act was the fact that the minister was to report to the House 60 days after January 1 of every year. The last time we had a report was March 31, 1980. These reports should emphasize the problems with the implementation of the agreement. There is probably no way the minister could submit a report, because it would document all kinds of terrible situations and it would be an embarrassment to the government.
The fact that the minister is legally supposed to table reports and has not done so for two years put him in contempt of Parliament. This was brought to the attention of the Speaker last year by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River on a question of privilege. The Speaker ruled that there is no way she can sanction a minister's action or make him accountable. She said we would have to find other recourse. There does not seem to be any other recourse to make this minister responsible to Parliament. Maybe it will have to be public recourse.
Nothing happened after we heard this terrible story a year ago last spring. The Cree and the Inuit returned this spring with more of the same stories, most of them even worse. The Inuit told us about the great inadequacies of the education system in their area where 1,500 or 1,600 children can only go as far as grade eight. In many communities there are no opportunities to go to school at all. Sometimes school is held in small shacks.
Housing standards are completely unacceptable and hundreds of new houses are needed. We have heard stories of contaminated water and children who are still becoming sick. Tuberculosis is still raging in the area. A year ago I brought to the attention of the House the fact that there was T.B. in the area but virtually nothing has been done about it. Chief Diamond told us at the hearings a month ago that since we heard from him last year his wife has contracted T.B. I would like to quote a small sentence about the problem to let you know how bad it is. A Mr. Therien, a research agent from the community health department of the University of Laval, testified as follows:

It is commonly known that tuberculosis is a symptom of very poor health conditions. It is a Third World disease and should not be acceptable in this day and age in Canada.
When the Inuit delegation came before us they even added a new dimension to their disturbing testimony. They told us of double standards where white people who came to work in their communities were put in good houses with running water and sewage systems while the native people had to live in shacks, many times with two to three families in small 14 by 18 rooms. Interestingly enough, just to illustrate the attitude of the department in its implementation of this act, I found out today that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has launched a legal suit in Quebec City against the James Bay Cree, and the school board in particular, for failure to pay their electrical bills. The Cree have launched a counter-suit against the department for not fulfilling its obligation to pay for the board of students who go out of the area to attend school.
This is an example of what is happening. An act was passed which was intended to prevent all this from happening. It was supposed to provide schooling, health care, housing, fire protection and air strips. 1 suggest that it is unacceptable for all of this to occur.
Last week i received a letter from a law firm which represents the Inuit people. I quote from it:
On behalf of the northern Quebec Inuit, and, in particular, Mrs. Mary Simon, president of Makivik Corporation-
And he mentions other people.

We would, therefore, again urge that the Committee make the strongest possible intervention at this time in light of the testimony by northern Quebec Inuit and the James Bay Crees concerning conditions in their communities resulting directly from the lack of implementation of the letter and spirit of Canada's obligations under the agreement.
This agreement was supposed to be a landmark agreement which would set the stage for all the land settlements across the country. It has not done that. Instead, it will make it more difficult to settle land claims.
Hon. members have heard my colleague from Prince George-Peace River refer to the standing committee hearings in Vancouver last month. That was to keep them in line. I find that completely unacceptable.

I have spoken of the situation in Quebec but the same problems are rampant in my own province. Time and again I have drawn to the attention of the minister and the bureaucrats the problems of the Mount Currie band in my riding. This band consists of approximately 1,000 people who have not had any new homes built for about four years. The reason for that is that the village sits on a flood plain at the present time, and it would require approximately 11 feet of fill to bring it above the flood plain. Since it is on a flood plain, CMHC will not give that band any money for mortgages. Therefore, the native people decided to move up on to a bench above the village and build a new subdivision. They have been working on this plan for years and had decided not to build any more houses on the lower area until the subdivision is ready. In the meantime there have been 13 fires and a number of deaths. The school has been condemned three times. They are still waiting for this subdivision to be approved. They have been promised it time and again. These are the same people who were instrumental in starting the sit-in at the regional office last year in Vancouver because of their frustration.
1 received a telex from them three days ago which I do not have time to read now. Nothing has happened despite the assurances 1 have had time and time again from the minister and his officials that they were going to address this serious problem.
These situations exist all across the country. I urge the minister to accept his responsibilities and do something about them. We are willing to help. He must keep his commitments to us and the native people of Canada because, if he does not, 1 am fearful that real trouble will erupt with the Indian people. They will no longer stand for the treatment they are receiving from this minister and this government.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking in today's debate in response to a moral obligation to be involved in an area of our nation's business from which it is all too easy to remain aloof. It is very easy for politicians and the public in general to dismiss responsibilities of the nation with respect to the aboriginal peoples as somehow less important when judged in the light of the total Canadian problem. I have myself had a very peripheral concern for this area of national affairs, and I say this to my shame, not my credit.
National apathy has demonstrated itself in the indifference which has permitted the unchallenged development of a selfcongratulatory attitude within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which unfortunately has resulted in neither addressing the interests of the native people nor the interests of Canadians. This is the great tragedy.
We see that the dominant interest being maintained and promoted is that of the bureaucrat to increase and expand the influence of his own empire which, in some instances, is a very large empire indeed. This is an agency of government in which the minister carries tremendous trust responsibilities for the wellbeing of a group of people who are generally threatened by a social and economic system which is opposed to their own traditional values. It is an agency of government whose failure in its purpose and its visionary but difficult opportunity is borne out by the repeated testimony of failure which came to
the standing committee and was spoken about by native people across the province. This is a very sad commentary on the conduct of the minister acting as a representative of the Crown. The final responsibility does rest solely on his shoulders. This is an essential part of the portfolio. If there ever was a time when there was a requirement for parternalism for native people, that time has passed. The time now is for assisted autonomy in which an advisory, financial and management-oriented autonomy must characterize the departmental thrust.
There is no place in it by which directives are impinged upon responsible decisions of band councils and chiefs. On the other hand, there is equally no place in a departmental policy that places unrestricted and undisciplined autonomy in the hands of those local band authorities without any final degree of accountability to the minister for their actions.
I am not impressed by the minister who shelters himself from his responsibility by saying, "I have given that responsibility and that authority to the band council to accept in any way they see fit. I have no responsibility for their actions; I only sign their bylaws. It is really not up to me after that."
The minister just cannot wash his hands of liability for events occurring on Indian property which comes under his charge. I just cannot accept it that the minister has no accountability for the carrying out of the terms of contracts made with the Crown. It is entirely convenient for the minister to say, as he did in a letter to myself dated June 3, 1982, the following:
It is up to the courts to determine when a band council has exceeded its authority.
The minister does not appear to understand his responsibility to individuals and enterprises which have entered into lease agreements with the Crown on the assumption that contracts made with the Crown would be managed by the Crown with an element of good faith. At the very least, the minister, through his department, must monitor the administrative faithfulness to the terms of each contract. Certainly when the minister has extended agent-of-the-Crown status to others, he must be responsive to grievances raised by either of the principal parties. Otherwise, the Crown itself will be brought into disrepute.

They rely completely on the integrity of the Crown, and quite rightly so. Likewise they rely on the integrity of the minister of the Crown, also quite rightly so. He says that suddenly this past policy has changed. He says it was changed without a word having been said to those Canadians who have invested millions of dollars in land projects. It was changed without their opinion being asked, without their thoughts on the matter being sought and, in fact, without any reference whatsoever having been made to it.
This gentleman said that it became known in 1981 that the minister had assigned the administration of these leases to the local band. He adds that he has handed over the administration to people who have a vested interest in every dollar they can obtain from those who have invested their lives in these reserve projects. He says there is without doubt a direct conflict of interest involved in this matter.
This gentleman then states that the confidence he and other businessmen had in the integrity of the Crown and of the minister is not being experienced in the relationship with the band council which the minister has appointed as the agents of the Crown. The minister is aware that some very serious allegations were made to him in a letter from that gentleman dated February 17, 1982. It is a very lengthy letter in which he went into great detail. Unfortunately, he received no response. That letter includes the following statement:
As long as the lease was being administered by the department, there were no problems. There was a good working relationship without conflict of any description.
All that this gentleman and others with similar perceived grievances are asking is that they be provided a forum, private and discreet, in which they can relate their experiences with confidence that their statements will be evaluated and that an appropriate response will be taken by the minister.
This is not unreasonable. It is not asking that the circumstances and the response be pre-judged and pre-arranged. It simply says to the minister that people are being hurt. They think they have a legitimate grievance. They want to tell the minister and his officials personally that they do not think it appropriate or practical to take every instance to the courts.

Peoples, for its tolerance of the miserable conditions existing in native communities throughout Canada which are of a standard vastly inferior to those found in most Third World Countries, for the Minister's failure to exercise his obligatory trust responsibility, and for the minister's contempt of Parliament as manifested by his deliberate refusal to comply with the statutory obligations which legally require him to report to the House on the progress of the implementation of the James Bay agreement.

Mr. Speaker, when I began my speech a few minutes before six o'clock I was expressing a word of tribute to the hard-working and dedicated Members of Parliament who serve on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They come from all three parties, and without exception they serve on this committee with the very best of motives. They understand and care about the issues and concerns brought before us. This is not a committee which can be manipulated or used by anyone.
Hear, hear!

This committee is not a tool of the government or the opposition, nor is it a tool of any one Indian organization or group of organizations. The members of this committee are more than sympathetically disposed to the aboriginal peoples of Canada, but we make our own objective evaluation of matters we should pursue and issues into which we should inquire. Let me say parenthetically that I hope that before this Parliament has concluded its work there will be very significant reform of our committee system.
Hear, hear!

But within the limits imposed upon all committees we have shown ourselves to be determined and independently minded. There may be, Mr. Speaker, committees of this House which are as good, but I doubt there is a committee which is any better.
The Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development now has a national constituency of aboriginal peoples who see it as a forum in which they can receive a fair, open and sympathetic hearing, and from which positive action can result. We can and do respond. For example, consider the case of the James Bay and Northern Quebec agreement. Last year the committee heard telling testimony of the failure of two governments, Canada's and Quebec's, to implement fairly the terms of this major historic agreement. It is futile here and now to argue whether strict legal obligations were or were not met; but clearly there was a failure to implement the spirit of the agreement. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) concurred in this conclusion. He, of course, was not the minister who either negotiated or signed the agreement, but his concern over this failure, in my view, merits full recognition. The minister agreed there were shortcomings, and he did something about them. He assigned senior officials to examine the problem in-depth and prepare a report. In addition, he went to the communities of James Bay in the company of the committee chairman and the local Member of Parliament, the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Gingras), who also serves as the vice-chairman of the committee. He saw for himself what the conditions were, and the disappointments in
this area where the agreement was supposed to have brought a new day.
In preparing the report I mentioned there were consultations with the James Bay Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit, and finally the so-called Tait report emerged with recommendations which are now awaiting cabinet approval. The James Bay Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit are anxious to know what moneys will be provided to fairly, decently and fully carry out the provisions of this historic agreement. It is most important in my mind and in the minds of all members of the standing committee that this cabinet decision be announced soon.
The standing committee, in its fifth report, Item No. 12, stated:
Recalling your committee's earlier report to the minister respecting the implementation of the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement, your committee is dismayed by the delay of the federal cabinet in reaching a just decision based on the recommendations of the department's review, providing for adequate funding according to the terms and conditions of the agreement.
We, on the committee, are anxious to see a fair and just settlement of this agreement for its own sake, but also because we know that it will have a significant effect on other land claims negotiations. There are important lessons to be learned from the James Bay agreement. Those who settle future claims will want to be assured of an adequate and workable implementation process. They will want to know that there are sufficient moneys to carry out the commitments expressed in these agreements or settlements. The comprehensive claims under negotiation north of 60 will require substantial sums of money. One way to ensure that these moneys are available would be to set aside a share of northern resource revenues in a trust fund for the future settlement of the very large comprehensive claims. This approach, among others, requires careful examination.
The motion of my friend, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) mentions the miserable conditions that exist in native communities across Canada. The government acknowledges that these conditions do exist and they are serious. The progress made in alleviating these conditions has been dismally slow. Today in Canada there are 300,000 Indian people in 573 bands. About 65 per cent of the Indian population is located in rural or remote communities. It is true that expenditures such as this year's commitment of $1 billion have, to some extent, improved Indian living conditions in material ways.
Those of us who have Indian reserves in our constituencies know that there have been some improvements. Housing has improved somewhat. Water and other community services are better and more plentiful. Health care and social services are more accessible to those in need. But in saying that, we must also be cognizant of the fact that the standard of living of the people of Canada as a whole has improved at an accelerated rate, and the gap between national standards and those of Indian people has not narrowed. For example, the life expectancy among Indian people is ten years less than the national average. There are more violent deaths and suicides among
June 17, 1982

Indian people. The number of Indian people on social assistance has increased.
Many of these conditions are described in a 1980 Department of Indian Affairs study entitled "Indian Conditions: A survey". In the area of housing, which has been of great concern to the standing committee, the study indicated that there was a backlog of 11,000 new houses. The study also stated that an additional 9,000 houses were desperately in need of repair. Last fall in a discussion paper on Indian housing, the department expressed the need for the same number of new houses, that is 11,000, but the number of houses needing renovation has also risen to 11,000. At the present time, one in every three Indian families lives in unacceptably crowded conditions.
Why do these conditions exist? I am sure a long list of reasons could be given, but they exist partly because there is a lack of an independent economic base in many Indian communities. That is so because so many of these communities are located in isolated and remote regions of this country. What of social assistance? Much of that $1 billion is directed toward social assistance, but social assistance is both a blessing and a curse. It provides for life's necessities, that is true, but at the same time it reinforces a sense of dependency. The Indian people do not like that sense of dependency any more than any other person in this country who does not want to be dependent upon someone else, on handouts, or to be beholden to the government for his or her wellbeing and existence.
Constitutionally, it is now recognized that there are aboriginal rights. The treaties are one expression of the unique relationship Indian people have with the Government of Canada. That relationship needs to be defined, it needs to be expanded. Our new Constitution calls for this to be done on a priority basis. I hope the aboriginal people of Canada will not be disappointed in the result of that endeavour because the Government of Canada has obligations to meet and grievances to settle.
1 have already referred to the comprehensive claims north of 60. There are the specific claims in the provinces which result from a long list of treaty violations. There is also the obligation to foster economic development and to restore self-reliance among Indian people. The latter calls for us to work with Indian leaders toward the establishment of effective Indian government for Indian people within the context of the Canadian confederation. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River when he said we are not talking here about a state within a state. We are talking about Indian government for Indian people within the context of the Canadian confederation. But we seem at times to be moving at a snail's pace, and the impatience with this slow progress is growing. The time is now for what the Chinese people once referred to in their development as a "great leap forward". That is what we need, a great leap forward in the area of government-Indian relations in Canada.
A few years ago I was reading an interesting book by Theodore H. White entitled "In Search of History". Incidentally Ted White is an author and a newspaperman who made
Supply
his reputation by doing an in-depth analysis of U.S. presidential elections. In the final chapter of White's book "In Search of History", he dealt with the administration of John F. Kennedy. The chapter is entitled "Camelot". I was struck by White's description of the manner in which President Kennedy advanced the cause of civil rights in the United States.
In 1963, President Kennedy announced to the American people that he had drafted a new civil rights bill. His speech to the nation had a single message: the need of new laws for new times. According to White, that legislation carried the concept of civil rights light years forward. The civil rights bill which became law in 1964 was revolutionary in a legislative and social sense.
In Canada, our relationship with our aboriginal peoples needs a similar momentum, that is, a great leap forward. We need to move light years ahead, even to be revolutionary. Instead, from our observations in the standing committee where a lot of frustration and impatience is absorbed from those who appear before us, we seem to be moving with reluctance and lethargy; without courage, imagination and vision. Our approach to Indian people and our relationship with them as a government, as we all know, has evolved from one of internal colonialism to attempted, but failed, assimilation, to the now cautious uncertain recognition that some form of limited, prescribed self-government must be accepted. In the past, giving Indian people special status and having them settle on specific land areas known as reserves really derived from a perceived need to protect Indians and Indian lands from exploitation by non-Indians. That was the motivation. It had nothing whatsoever to do with an understanding of, or a respect for, the treaties. In fact, it was nothing more than a policy of internal colonialism.
In 1969 the policy which had been with us for so long was changed, and the much-heralded white paper on Indian policy was tabled in the House. In case hon. members do not know or do not remember, I remind them that politicians from all political parties thought that the paper represented very significant progress. The spokesmen for each political party, if hon. members check the record of Hansard, thought that it was a step forward.
We will look.
Please do.
We have learned since then.

Hon. members opposite have learned and we have learned, but let me remind my hon. friends how we have learned. We should not pat ourselves on the back. We learned because the Indian people themselves perceived that this was a policy of assimilation which meant for them cultural genocide.
Over the past several years, self-government has emerged as a pivotal concern in the quest by Canada's Indian peoples for a redefined role within confederation. For them self-government is inextricably linked to the achievement of self-determination and the preservation of their cultural heritage. Increased political activity by Indian associations has forced federal officials to move Indian policy a little more in line with actual

June 17, 1982
Supply
political, economical and social development of many Indians in Canada. But, according to a recent study, the bringing of Indian policies more in line with current development has been espoused in order to head off larger and more intense challenges in the future. There is something of a stalling tactic involved here.
These new uncharted waters to which I have referred are being avoided because it is known that additional moneys will need to be appropriated. When we have a large and growing federal deficit, that is not a very appealing idea. It may require the reallocation of funds and resources within government, and we all know the kinds of difficulties which that can create. What would happen to the present control mechanism operated by the department? How could accountability be assured? My committee believes that we should confront these issues squarely, not run away from them or hide. Therefore, we requested in our famous fifth report a special reference from Parliament to examine the total financial and other relationships of the Government of Canada with Indian and Inuit people. It is my conviction that the committee, if given this responsibility, could very greatly assist the government by indicating what the desirable goals are and what new directions we must follow in order to get there.
All the wisdom in the world does not reside with our public officials.

Agreed.
