I appreciate the graciousness of the House in giving me a few more minutes to conclude.
As I was saying, those of us who have dialogued with Indian people for many years could, given the time and with thoughtful consultation, offer some acceptable and exciting new policy options which would be genuinely progressive.
The language of the motion before us this evening is in the traditional partisan, adversarial mould. I do not think it upsets any one of us too much. After all, this is Parliament; it is not a club for ladies and gentlemen. This is not a place for Mr. and Mrs. Milque-toast. This is Parliament, raw in tooth and claw, so no one is easily upset or disturbed. It is true that it condemns the government and the minister. It speaks of tolerating miserable conditions and of failures to meet objectives and to comply. If we put that somewhat offensive phraseology aside, it can be agreed that we must make a new beginning. We must make a fresh start and we must do so with some vigour and conviction.
Earlier I said that the constitutional conference on aboriginal rights could be such a commencement, but 1 say to the House that the standing committee could be of service in moving us light years ahead in the renewal of government-Indian relationships. Indian people and their leaders are ready and willing to get the process under way. Enlightened Canadians from across the country are looking to us for results. Finally, the world is watching and our credibility in the international community is at stake. We must not fail to act decisively and to do so without delay.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak to the motion tonight. There are many things to say when one rises to speak on a subject which is not often discussed in the House at a time when many groups and individuals from bands across the country have come to Parliament to indicate the difficulties with which they are faced. Before commencing the speech I should like to give this evening, I say to the hon. member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) that we appreciate the way in which he conducts the committee. If we have a chairman who assists the committee in its work, it is easier for all parties to do the best job possible in helping people. That is really what this debate is all about.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) has a difficult job. In a sense, he is always dealing with people, and he has a restricted budget which has not grown perhaps as fast as we would like, given present difficulties. Of course, he must work within that budget. Many of us on this side honestly believe that there are ways of improving the expenditures of the minister and his department.
We have mentioned in our motion a number of things which are upsetting to us as a party. One area which is constantly a problem is the fact that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is still in place and that the minister, because of that, has a distinct trust relationship with native people. Because of that trust relationship, one would think that the Indian people themselves would have a certain trust. However, we find instead many cases of Indian band representatives across Canada coming to Ottawa day after day, week after week, coming to the House to tell us, Members of Parliament, that they do not in fact trust the manner in which expenditures are being made on their behalf. They are spending their money to travel here because promises have been made but have not been fulfilled.
Conditions on reserves are worse than conditions in Third World countries. Native people are coming to Ottawa in the hope that we, as Members of Parliament, the minister and his officials, will listen to their plea and act upon it. Native people who do not have much money hire consultants to help them with their pleas. They are spending millions of dollars each year. Why do native people have to hire consultants? The

June 17, 1982

department is supposed to be there, surely, to fulfil that function itself and assist the native people in expanding their livelihood. The natives do not hire consultants to advise them on how to build houses; they hire political consultants to help get the minister's attention to deal with things that they believe are essential to their reserves. Native people themselves are worried about the necessity of hiring consultants. Last year, political advisers in one province took up more than $1 million of native funds to help with such things as conducting marches and preparing briefs. They do this because when they go to the officials in the capital cities or the regional directors in other areas to ask for commitments they usually get no for an answer. However, when they deliver those requests in the form of a concise report or attractive brief they often get yes for an answer. Therefore, they spend money on obtaining the assistance of consultants. Much of this money is wasted, something which they cannot afford to do.
I would like to read a comment by a chief of an Indian band. This appeared in the Edmonton Journal. He was asked why they do this, and he said:
Take a band that has lived through 50 years of frustration. If you go in there and give them hope of any kind, they'll ride that hope right down the tube.
That is why they hire consultants.
1 have been speaking of a trust relationship wherein the minister has certain funds. There must be a trust that he will spend that money properly. Many native people in Canada do not believe that it is being spent properly. The department should be working itself out of a job instead of increasing the numbers of people working in the department and using funds which are desperately needed to assist native people.
Since the minister is a lawyer I realize that he wishes every word to be taken strictly in the legal sense. There is now a new funding procedure for the use of the bands own money. Instead of the traditional method of Indian bands' presenting a yearly funding proposal to the minister for the use of their own money, they now have to present that proposal every three months. The minister has said that this must be done because it is in line with his trust responsibility. No business can operate when it does not know what its funding will be three months in the future. In fact, in order to have the three-month spending requisition, they have to send in a new requisition each month. In my opinion, instead of assisting native people, we are moving back to the ancient concept where the department knows best how native people can fund themselves with their own money which is in their trust funds. There is some $500 million in those trust funds which should be used to assist native people.
Why has this funding proposal been changed? The department has said that the management system has encouraged the department to place a sharper emphasis on structured, formalized planning than ever before. Believe me, departments of this government know best how to structure and how to formalize planning. This is one of the difficulties that the native people have.
The hon. member for Cochrane-Superior defined some of the health and social problems that native people are facing as compared with those faced by the non-native society. He said
Supply
that the mortality rates were significantly higher. This was mentioned as well by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) with respect to the health problems experienced in northern Quebec. The death rate of infants due to infectious disease is very high. Indians use hospital facilities two to two and a half times more often than the national average. In 1977 there were 1,200 families living in condemned houses. One out of every four reserve houses are in need of repair. Incomes are half the national average, and welfare dependancy on some reserves reaches 70 per cent. Is it any wonder that we suggest that conditions on many of our reserves are worse than in many Third World countries which we are, quite properly, helping?
I reviewed the recommendations of CIDA to see if assistance could be made available by that organization. It is interesting to note that CIDA is capable of operating also in Canada under its terms of reference. It is common knowledge that CIDA carries on successful projects in other countries. Perhaps it might be incumbent upon the minister to ask CIDA for assistance in order to improve the poor conditions which we have described. Perhaps funding could be provided through their expertise to assist native people, instead of providing them with such things on new housing as the so-called J circulars.
When there is a shortage of some 11,000 homes in Canada for native people, with almost as many homes that are condemned or in desperate need of repair, we now see a new housing policy which says that the government will provide $18,000 to $22,000 on condition that a certain amount of the natives' own money is added to finish building the homes. It does not makes good sense to tell a native family who is on welfare and barely able to feed and clothe itself to add its own money. Where will they get the extra money from?
Some chiefs and councils have said it is impossible for them to build a home on that amount of money, but since they have been allocated money for the construction of ten or 12 houses they will pool the money instead and build five houses. But the government says, "No. If you do that, we will take all the money back.'' This is the situation which results from the new J circulars which are being handed out throughout Canada. As a result, no housing projects, or very few, are proceeding this spring.
If we look at the budget that has been spent for housing in Canada for the last ten years, we see that it adds up to some $700 million, if I read the estimates correctly. If that amount were divided among the number of native families in this country we should have been able to build one house for every family. Yet we are behind by 11,000.
There are some serious questions which must be asked about the housing policy and why house construction is so far behind. The minister has access to something called the Western Development Fund which is supposedly to be used to help in the construction of houses. Western Canada is happy to provide that money if, in fact it goes to building houses since many native people reside in the west. It is my hope that this

June 17, 1982
Supply
money will quickly be put to use and that this new circular being distributed will be amended.
The department also has something called "paper houses". Officials of the department indicate how many houses are to be built under this plan. In many cases the bank is in debt. They do not have a sufficient amount of money to fund other programs. Therefore, they pull it out of the housing project. The department tells them to pull it out of there. No one mentions that the homes are not built. Unless they are actually counted, the department assumes the homes have actually been built. As a result, we have something called "paper houses". Perhaps we are short even more than the anticipated
11,000	homes.
We are not being given a lot of time to speak today. That is good because it gives more members an opportunity to speak. I would like to deal with one other subject before closing. It is important to the Indian people of this country. They have their rights entrenched in the Constitution. A great deal of time was spent on this in the last year before the Constitution was brought home to this nation. Within a year of last April, a conference must be called to deal with the definition of aboriginal rights. Because there is only one year, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about this. It is a difficult question. I wanted to know what the federal government feels it ought to be doing. Have the federal government and the minister been in touch with the Indian leadership in this nation to have preliminary meetings so that there are no surprises when the conference is called? If the conference fails, does that mean the constitutional requirement has been settled? If we have no definition, do we carry on as before? When I asked the Prime Minister about this, he said no. He felt that the first step would be to consult the provinces to get their view as to a date for the meeting and as to what groups they would like to see invited.
That simply is not good enough. The minister ought to be meeting with Indian groups across this country now. He should be stating what his position is with regard to this constitutional conference. The provinces should be made aware of the direction in which the government and the native people feel we should be going. At the present time, we have not heard anything about the position of this government on the constitutional conference and the role it feels it should play in it.
Members have spoken of difficulties. They have appreciated having the opportunity to do that. I would point out that education is essential if young people are to help their bands. Many accomplishments have been made in this area. Economic development is essential to get people off welfare so that they can be productive and have pride in themselves. Economic development spending involves some SI00 million. Social assistance spending is almost $300 million. The hon. member for Cochrane-Superior spoke about that. It is important that we get more money into the economic development area so
that people can carry out productive work and again take pride in themselves.
It is not often that we get to speak on the issue of our Indian people. This opposition day has provided us with that opportunity. I hope the minister is now aware of some of the criticisms being laid at his feet and some of the responsibilities he must carry out in the next number of months.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to contribute to this debate, especially since part of the motion now under consideration deals with the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement, an area which is part of my constituency. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall briefly the background of this question in order to better understand how the James Bay agreement came about and the problems caused by its implementation. It will then be easier to understand, Mr. Speaker, that the James Bay area, which is nearly totally included in the Abitibi riding which I represent, is different from every other region in Canada. These differences explain the philosophy under which this unique and unprecedented agreement was negotiated.
As we all know, the James Bay territory was purchased by the Government of Canada from the Hudson's Bay Company. The region was then called Rupert's Land. I have here an order in council from 1898 which gave part of this territory to the province of Quebec. In 1912, the rest of the territory was handed over to Quebec. To give you an idea of its geographic location, my native town of Amos was given to the province of Quebec in 1898. This territory extended to the middle of the Eastmain River. In 1912, the territory of the province of Quebec was extended to include the entire territory from the upper part of the Eastmain River to the northern boundary. However, at the same time, Quebec had to take responsibility for territorial matters and other issues concerning the native people, their interests and their claims, which were completely non-existent in the Abitibi territory from 1898 until quite recently, around 1960. It is only at that time that the province of Quebec decided to integrate Abitibi into its administrative map.
In the report of the Dorion commission on the integrity of the Quebec territory, Mr. Justice Dorion recommended: That the Quebec government take action immediately to honor the commitments made toward the Indians in the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912. He also recommended: That this commitment be kept by means of an agreement between the Quebec government and the duly appointed representatives of the Indian bands of Quebec, to be ratified by the government of Canada. I emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker, to show what problems we expected when this agreement was signed. Around 1970, the province of Quebec started to show some interest in northern Quebec and to build dams and roads, and it is only with the James Bay dam project that, following
June 17, 1982

representations by the Crees and the Inuits, Quebec agreed to sit down, after all the problems caused by court proceedings, land claims and work shutdowns on the James Bay project, and try to negotiate an agreement.
That agreement dating back to 1975, that is contained in this document, was negotiated from 1973 to 1975. Who were the parties to that agreement? We find on page VII that the agreement was between the Government of Quebec, the Societe d'energie de la Baie James, the Societe de developpe-ment de la Baie James, the Commission hydroelectrique du Quebec (Hydro-Quebec) the Grand Council of Crees and Inuits of Quebec, and finally the Government of Canada. It will be remembered that Mr. John Ciaccia was Premier Bourassa's official representative at those negotiations. We find at the beginning of the agreement certain facts that are quite amazing in the light of today's situation. Mr. Ciaccia explained to members of the National Assembly in Quebec, on November 5, 1975, the philosophy of that agreement which clearly shows the shared responsibilities in the development of James Bay. 1 would like to quote excerpts from his speech that are very telling. On page XI, Mr. Ciaccia stated, and I quote:
That agreement enables us to accomplish two great tasks to which our government was committed.
"Our government" means the Quebec government.
It enables us-
-the agreement-
-to fulfil our responsibilities towards the people in our northern areas and finally to have a Quebec presence in all the territories included within our geographical boundaries.
Those geographical boundaries, Mr. Speaker, are those that were established in 1898 and 1912.
Mr. Ciaccia went on to say:
But along with that acquisition, Quebec assumed the responsibility to settle a number of land claims and other issues involving the native people, such as their interests and claims.
It was a recognition that the province of Quebec was involved in the James Bay Indians' claims. I said earlier that the province of Quebec had not included that territory in its administrative map. It should be kept in mind that the province of Quebec had nothing to do whatsoever with the James Bay and Hudson Bay territories. Schools were under federal jurisdiction, contrary to the Constitution. The federal government was responsible for health and police services and, to further quote Mr. Ciaccia:
People in northern Quebec need schools like everyone else. They must be able to rely on health services. They must be in a position to bring their differences before fair-minded judges and have the institutions needed to enforce the law. The agreement meets these various needs and provides the necessary structures. We-
-the Government of Quebec-
Supply
-will establish local school boards, social services and health boards, police and fire departments, municipal courts, and these institutions will come under the relevant departments of the Government of Quebec.
And he went on to say:
And all those services will be provided through the facilities of the Quebec government.
In other words, any services such as schools and hospitals under federal jurisdiction which the native communities may have already will become Quebec's responsibility. The Quebec government will take over some of the existing federal programs. Mr. Speaker, 1 think I have said enough to show that the implementation of the James Bay Agreement is not strictly a federal issue. In the last pages appear the names of the signatories, while the parties to the agreement are listed at the beginning. As I said earlier, that agreement was unique and unprecedented. It was inspired by principles which I tried to single out in the remarks of Mr. Caccia whom I quoted a moment ago, there were problems in its implementation, and a great many terms in the wording of that agreement were rather ambiguous. There were certain steps which Hydro-Quebec as well as the governments of Quebec and Ottawa were supposed to take. So after six years we ended up without any implementation mechanism.
When I was elected in 1980, I was contacted almost immediately by Mr. Billy Diamond-who was and still is Grand Chief of the Grand Council of the Crees-and Northern Quebec Inuit Association President Charlie Watt. Both had signed the James Bay Agreement and they wanted to try to set that agreement straight. In 1981, in February or March,
I believe, I was a member of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development when spokesmen for the Grand Council of the Crees and the Inuit of Northern Quebec appeared before us to submit a brief in which they claimed that some things needed improvement in the implementation of the James Bay Agreement.
Mr. Speaker, we must bear in mind that the agreement had been signed in 1975 by the Bourassa government and that on November 15, 1976, a whole new team took over in Quebec City. Most of the contents of that document flowed from an agreement and discussions between the federal government, the PQ government which was then in power, the Crees and the Inuit. There is no need for me to spell it out, Mr. Speaker. Let us recall the situation in 1976 and it will be readily seen that the discussions aimed at implementing that agreement were rather strained because of the Quebec-Canada policies. The Quebec government was not paying much attention to native culture. It had no expertise in native matters. And, following these claims, I am grateful to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) who agreed to lend one of his senior officials to look into the James Bay development problem.

June 17, 1982

Now, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say, because of my privileged position both as a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and as member for that riding, that the government has responded favourably to the concerns of the committee as well as to those of the Crees and Inuits of the James Bay area. The enquiry, consultation and decision-making processes, which started in March, 1981, proved long and sometimes painful to all parties involved, but I feel that it was not an exercise in futility. On several occasions, the minister indicated in this House that a decision concerning the James Bay question was forthcoming. During its proceedings, the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Affairs raised also the issue of an annual report to be tabled in Parliament on the implementation of the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement. People are aware that such a document has not yet been tabled by the minister. Surely the committee is right in stressing that that obligation has not been met. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, people are also aware that the tabling is undoubtedly linked with the completion of that study. Why table only part of a report on the implementation of the James Bay agreement if the study of this implementation is not yet completed. I am sure that the government intends to remedy this situation and will make sure that all future annual reports are tabled on time.
Hon. members opposite should appreciate, however, that since this very meticulous study was carried out over the past 18 months, it would have been difficult, if not outright impossible, to table a report which would reflect a rapidly changing situation. I know that the minister has asked for the understanding of Indian groups and the House in this respect. Hon. members are indeed aware that the Standing Committee has been looking into this matter for quite a while and that it issued a special statement in March, 1981. I can now inform the House that the minister will contact the Cree and Inuit leaders within the next few days or very shortly to examine with them the Standing Committee's findings.
Briefly, I would like to draw the attention of the House on the process-

I wish to thank my colleagues for their cooperation. I still have about a minute and a half to go. I mention the fact because I consider such an approach as a typical example of the co-operation which can exist between
the government and native groups in finding common solutions. Of course, this analysis of the James Bay agreement is not and was not intended to be a magic formula. No doubt some other obstacles will crop up. However, I think that if we maintain this same attitude, this openmindedness, we will finally find a more adequate response in a more serene atmosphere. Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much for the congenial spirit of this House and I will now end my remarks.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my thanks to all hon. members in the House who have spoken on behalf of natives. I too would like to give my support to this motion. The only problem I have is in knowing where to begin. I have the feeling that with a department such as the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development wherever one chooses to shoot, one can likely hit a target. For an opposition critic looking for ammunition against the government this department emerges as a veritable ammunition dump. Because the department is open to criticism on so many fronts, it would be impossible to touch on everything in one brief speech.
The barn door of Canadian politics.

Or an igloo! What I will do, then, is to focus on one aspect of DIAND's mandate which is of particular interest to me and the people I represent. I will leave it to my colleagues in the House to address the many other issues which can legitimately be raised.
What I would like to focus on is this government's policy on native land claims, a matter for which DIAND is responsible.
I would like to give a brief history of how and why the government's policies on claims have failed to serve the needs of northern peoples as well as other native peoples in this country.
Before dealing with the situation as it is today, let me explain briefly why the government even deals with the issue of claims and how it has handled them in the past. In the first place, the government has been obliged to deal with claims because the British legal tradition requires that native interests in any lands be recognized and dealt with before any nonnatives begin to use it. The way the federal government has always done this has been to make treaties with the native peoples and extinguish their rights in exchange for some type of compensation. When we look back over the history of treaty making, it is easy to see patterns emerge. It is easy to see, for example, that the treaties were designed to serve the needs of other people more than the needs of the natives themselves. The government's primary motivation for dealing with native peoples has always been to clear the way for development, either agricultural, non-renewable or otherwise. This was the pattern which prevailed across the prairies in the years immediately after confederation, with the construction of the CPR and the opening up of the west for farming. That is not to condemn those vocations. Indian peoples were pushed aside in
June 17, 1982

the quest for land, and the treaty-making process was meant to give it a semblance of legitimacy.
The economic and renewable resource base of the native people on the prairies, the buffalo, was eliminated, and the native people were left with the option of either being assimilated into the new society or being segregated onto reserves. Either way would leave them marginalized, culturally, economically, politically, socially and otherwise.
Perhaps the most painful lesson that native people learned about the government during this period was the fact that it was prepared to use military force to quell any resistance to this marginalization process.
Only a few such treaties have ever been signed in what can properly be called the north and, unfortunately, the same pattern has emerged. Treaty No. 8 was signed in the Upper Mackenzie Valley in 1898 in order to accommodate the influx of non-natives attracted north by the Yukon gold rush. The government felt no need to settle any other claims in this area, until oil was discovered at Norman Wells in 1920. Within the year, Treaty No. 11 was signed. The government's interest obviously had more to do with securing legal control of the oil resources at Norman Wells than it did with protecting the interest of the local residents. By the 1920s most of the likely areas of settlement or development in Canada were covered by treaties, and so the process came to a halt for about 50 years.
By the late 1960s the tragic consequences of this type of approach were painfully obvious to most Canadians. Native people suffered from the highest rates of infant mortality, school dropouts, unemployment, alcoholism and, not surprisingly, suicide. This situation continues today.
While the strategy of pushing native people aside had served its short-term purpose in the nineteenth century, by the midtwentieth century its social consequences were proving to be enormous. One would like to think that, when faced with the prospect of opening up yet another frontier area the government would now be willing, if not eager, to find an alternative approach to the land claims-an approach that would not have such tragic consequences for the people involved or such enormous long-term costs for the country as a whole.
One would like to think that the government would be interested in learning from its past mistakes, but as a close observer of the government's action in this field I have to report that it has not. This is what the government must be condemned for-not being willing to alter its modern-day approach to the issue from the one it pursued in the past, despite its obvious long-term consequences.
When 1 speak about the government's latter day approach, I am referring to the policies it has adopted in this last decade to deal with outstanding native claims, primarily in the north. The 1970s witnessed the dawn of a new era of frontier expansion and exploration in Canada. The north has become the focus, and the search for energy has become the driving force. As with the earlier frontiers, this drive to open up new regions
Supply
carried with it the responsibility for dealing somehow with the northern peoples' claim in the lands in question.
At the outset of the 1970s, when development pressures were just beginning to emerge, the government actually felt that it could ignore the whole issue of native claims because it felt the concept of aboriginal title had no legal basis. It was content to operate on this assumption and to let the native people use the courts to prove otherwise, if they could. In January 1973, the Supreme Court of Canada issued a historic decision on a question of whether the native rights of the Nishga had ever been extinguished. The fact that that court split 3-3 on this vital question gave the concept of native rights much more legal validity and it also rather stunned the government of the day. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) reacted to the decision by telling the Niska, "Perhaps you have more legal rights than we thought you had".
What this decision did was cause the government to reevaluate its approach to the whole claims question. It could no longer ignore the fact that native people might actually have a legal claim to the land, and that any future court case could now just as easily favour the native people. Instead of leaving it up to the courts then, because they were proving unreliable, the government had to take control of the settlement process itself so that it could control the timing and the results more effectively. This is what the 1973 policy statement was designed to do.
The government's whole approach to the settlement of native claims was conditioned by its other main priority, which was to clear the way for development. As long as ownership of the land remained uncertain, investors would not be attracted to the north. So, if the government wanted to get a pipeline built, it had to take responsibility for clarifying who owned the land. Extinguishing aboriginal claims was a way of doing that once and for all.
Faced, then, with having to settle claims, the government simply dusted off the policy that had been used so effectively in the previous century, and set out to repeat the same process all over again, this time in its last frontier, the north.
The 1973 policy statement established the policy which remains in effect to this day. Let me point out exactly what it was designed to do from the government's point of view, and I would suggest that if it is allowed to proceed, it will lead to the eventual marginalization of native people in the north as well.
First, the 1973 policy statement said that settlements of comprehensive claims should be achieved through negotiations. As I said, this was designed to get the issue out of the courts where decisions were not proving as favourable as the government would have liked. Second, it said that the complete and final extinguishment of native title would be the only acceptable outcome of the settlement process. Third, the sole purpose of the negotiation process would be to determine the type of compensation to be paid for the loss of those rights, plus the amount.
I am taking the time to go into detail on this because this policy reflects a great deal about the government's approach to

June 17, 1982
Supply
native peoples. While it is couched in much more sophisticated language, and there are much more elaborate structures in place for negotiating settlements than in the last century, I fear that its fundamental goals have remained essentially the same-to extinguish native peoples' rights to their land. And I also fear that if the policy is allowed to be repeated, so too will the consequences.
It is interesting to note what has happened between the government and the native groups in the north since this policy was introduced. The northern peoples have been quick to reject the premises of the 1973 policy, recognizing it for what it is- merely the nineteenth century policy resurrected. They have refused to accept their intended fate passively; they have rejected the government's approach and demanded that the door be opened to alternatives.
We realized early on, for example, that some land base was essential for our continued viability as a distinct people. Instead of having our rights to the land extinguished in a settlement, why could we not have them entrenched? Instead of having to choose between a traditional economy and a modern industrial one, why could we not have enough control over the pace of development that we might enjoy the benefits of both? Instead of having political decisions made for us, why can we not make our own, and have structures which reflect our own needs and values, and work these out with other people?
Throughout the 1970s the government did not prove very receptive to these kind of questions. It consistently refused to broaden the mandate of its negotiators, for example, to include questions of political rights. It preferred to keep it at the level of a simple real estate transaction, where a certain amount of money is exchanged for a certain amount of land, with some hunting and fishing rights thrown in. It has even gone so far as to set up separate commissions such as the one headed by the Prime Minister's friend, Mr. Drury, to ensure that such matters as political development cannot be discussed in the same forum as claims.
Despite this resistance, the native groups have gone ahead and developed their own alternatives to the "land for money" approach. The Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, for example, has submitted a proposal for the creation of Nunavut, a new territory in the eastern Arctic which would evolve into full provincial status over a period of up to 15 years. Support for this proposal is running high in the region right now, as illustrated by the overwhelming vote in favour of division in the recent plebiscite held on April 14 in the Northwest Territories. It is hoped that some action will be taken shortly to implement the results of that vote.
In the western Arctic, the Dene and Metis have also developed a vision of how things should be if their culture and economy are to be allowed to thrive. Their Denendeh proposal calls for political structures which would recognize the permanence of the native community in the area in the face of a
growing population of non-natives who may stay for only a short time.
Despite our consistent demand that new models for settlements have to be found, the federal government has still not really indicated much willingness to do so. In fact, in its first update of policy since 1973, the statement entitled "In all Fairness", the government seemed dead set on holding on to the policy objectives it outlined in 1973. Even though it now prefers to speak of an "exchange" of undefined rights for concrete rights and benefits, it still amounts to the same thing: extinguishment. Given the consistent opposition to extinguishment throughout the 1970s, one wonders where the government has been. It is this kind of stubborn insistence on the old way of doing things which is preventing speedy settlements in the north, and it is this stubborn refusal to seriously consider the alternatives which is greatly frustrating the people I represent, and which causes me to support this motion.
Evidence of the federal government's continuing bad faith I believe exists in the recent wildlife agreement, in principle initialled in Frobisher Bay on October 27, 1981, by federal government negotiators and the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada. For over seven months now the Inuit have been waiting for official endorsement of this agreement. But that is only the first stage in a comprehensive land claims agreement between the federal government and the Inuit of Canada, and we will be watching closely to determine whether the government is willing to act in honesty on our behalf. Therefore, I support this motion of the hon. member for Wataskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger).

2,000	votes.
Hear, hear!
That is the first time that the NDP has ever held that seat.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that had to be one of the most superficial and juvenile exploitations of the rules of order that I have heard for some time. I am sure the hon. member of the NDP who just spoke must have shrugged in utter embarrassment that we could be discussing the plight and poverty of the native peoples all day, and then the NDP, the sole possessor of social conscience, just dump their terrible concern and abuse the rules in order to interject something which is totally irrelevant to the discussion.

Hear, hear!
June 17, 1982

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
If the NDP can contain their glee for about 20 minutes while 1 make my remarks, I would appreciate it. I can only assume that they, like the official opposition, wish to hear the reply to questions they themselves have raised, so here they are.
First, Mr. Speaker, 1 feel very strongly that the standing committee has been a good committee. It is made up of members of all political parties, and therefore political life being what it is they will of necessity politicize their feelings and get the maximum impact as a result of the political position they take in the never ending partisanship which takes place. But in my experience that committee, perhaps more than in any other, has had a common theme amongst all members, one of very deep concern indeed for the wellbeing of the native peoples. It is shown by a basic sort of bipartisan approach when it really counts as far as achieving a given objective is concerned, and I think that speaks well not only for the committee but for Parliament itself. There is a very vivid and stark example of that, which is the James Bay matter which the committee wished to have rectified. I think all members will be happy to know that matter is probably soon to be rectified.
Having said that, I do not wish to attempt to correct a whole multitude of inaccuracies, but I will deal with some. I think some of these inaccuracies probably were stated in the exuberance of the point hon. members wished to make. If I thought that every Indian leader and every Indian person in Canada and the general public were going to read today's Hansard and study all the figures that were quoted, I would probably go to some considerable pains to correct each and every exuberance uttered. But I do not think I will do that. Of necessity, though, I should deal with some very briefly before making my other remarks.
The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) talked about administration, and about how funds are allocated not only generally but in the B.C. region. The reason I want to deal with that is that some of the charges are serious. I think the figures he has quoted show a lack of ability and capacity to understand the most basic facts about the bandfunding process. The hon. member is not here, so I trust some of his colleagues will make him aware of my reply to some of his serious charges.
We have tried to explain to the hon. member in committee the band-funding process for some time. Maybe he just wants to persist in the distortions despite these endless efforts to correct him. However, for the benefit of other members let me explain some of the major faults. As many members know, program services to any one band can be provided in three basic ways. First, bands can administer the entire program. This now covers about 50 per cent of the entire budget of the department. Second, some programs, and for a very few bands nearly all programs, are still delivered by the Department of Indian Affairs. This comprises about 25 per cent of the department's budget. Incidentally, that figure includes, in addition to a wide range of educational, social and other programs, all the department's administration costs. Finally, Mr. Speaker, some 25 per cent of the budget consists of
Supply
funding provided to provincial governments to provide education and social services to a large number of Indian communities. If you look at the dollars administered by the band, then, anyone can see that this will be very low indeed for bands which receive services directly from the department. They are not getting all the money for all the programs because the department is directly providing the services or the provincial governments are doing it. On the other hand, the figures will be very high for those bands who administer their own school and all other costly programs. If in a certain year they are building a large capital facility such as a water system or a school building, it will be very high. So if an analysis is done in a reasonable and fair way, without a calculated effort to distort, it will show that funds are allocated on a fair and equitable basis.
The blatant inference of the hon. member that somehow some bands, who have more influence than others have the ear of the department, and get a very high amount while other bands get a very low amount was made without taking into account the three different possible ways of delivering funds. What hon. members think of generalized distortions of the type resorted to by my friend, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River is for them to decide. Needless to say, I do not think very much of them.
As to the other question raised by some hon. members with respect to the principle of local government, let me just say that I think the department and 1 would carry out the concept of local government for Indian bands. This concept is one we heartily endorse. We endorse it in the sense that would cover a whole range of local governmental responsibilities to be taken over by a band council and not just in certain areas such as education and cultural activities with rather limited emphasis that I detected in what the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River said. We have had some considerable work done in this area. Along with the standing committee as an aid I hope to ascertain the feelings of the native people. I hope to discuss the matter at some future time with the chairman of the standing committee, and I hope to look into this whole question of consultation with respect to the ultimate devolution of far more responsibility at the option of the bands who wish to exercise this full range of government responsibility.
May I now move on to another area. Again, I think another very serious distortion was made, and it should be clarified. I believe the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River indicated that some bands had money for per capita distribution and that some evil, paternalistic minister of Indian affairs was residing some place and refusing to have per capita distribution made to minors under the age of 21. I think the hon. member used the word "starving" in that respect. That is ridiculous. What happens when a band has the money and its chief and band council, wish to make a per capita allocation under the act? There is no degree of volition on my part; it is subject to the advice of independent law officers of the Crown. Any minister would have to abide by the advice because of the

June 17, 1982
Supply
Canadian system of parliamentary government, whether he be an NDP minister of Indian affairs, a Conservative or a Liberal one. He would have to take that advice because ministers cannot give themselves legal advice. That legal advice is that the Canadian government and the minister of Indian affairs would be held accountable legally by any minor upon attaining the age of majority if the individual does not discharge his responsibility in a legal and proper way along the lines of the concept of a trustee. If a minister of Indian affairs turns over a per capita share to a minor as if he were an adult, perhaps turning it over to the parent, that child, upon attaining the age of 21, if the parent has misused the money and did not make it available to the child in the way it should have been made available, that child can sue the government for irresponsibility in turning over his per capita share to someone else when he was a minor, and recover it when he attains majority. Not only is the government held accountable for irresponsibility in the allocation of the per capita share legally, but the minor may not receive the money at all.
We have been able to find a compromise in the situation, with legal endorsement, in limited amounts of per capita share for minors, that is $250 a month or $3,000 per year per child. That can be turned over to parents and charged off against the per capita share of the minor. There is nothing paternalistic about this. There is no desire to starve some innocent Indian child, as was so exuberantly distorted by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River. It is certainly not based on any motivation to be paternalistic; it is based on a solid legal opinion.
1 must say that if there is a desire on the part of the standing committee or of members of the House to change that, they can change the Indian Act. Parliament can direct the Ministry of Justice to give legal opinions based on a legal statute. We do not have a different statute right now. We have the statute that Parliament last passed. I take it all hon. members want the statutes passed by this Parliament respected until they are changed.
I am now moving on to another area, again dealing with some of what I think are unfortunate distortions that arose relative to the British Columbia region. Again, I am referring to how serious some of the charges are. The following figures should be noted as far as the B.C. region is concerned. The region of B.C. has an on-reserve population of approximately 34,500 Indian people. In the year 1981-1982 a total of $101.2 million in grants and contributions, $4.7 million in capital facilities on reserves, $9,266,843 in child care and $21,322,615 was used for education payments under the master tuition agreement. These four items total $136,489,458, which, as anyone here would be prepared to acknowledge, represents a substantial commitment to the Indian people of British Columbia.
In order to indicate what is happening in that region with respect to the topic which the member opposite wishes to stress, that is, the level of program operation being undertaken by Indian bands themselves, let me tell you that in 1976, the department had over $20 million in British Columbia under
band control and less than 100 bands were operating programs. In addition, we have reduced, not increased, the department's regional staff to 559, while the number of band employees has grown less than 300 to 970. This rapid transfer of services is clear evidence that the region is not only sensitive to the needs and wishes of native people but is providing them with the needed tools for self-overnment.
Can we not take into account some of these additional factors before making some of the wide sweeping and I think dangerous allegations, almost bordering on smear, covering a whole group of people? Many of them are civil servants, both native and non-native, who should be given the benefit of the doubt, whose good intentions should not be doubted. Many of them are well motivated, as perhaps many Members of Parliament are, and because they are public servants they cannot defend or speak for themselves.
It is getting to be rather ritualistic. If my predecessor in this portfolio were here with a Liberal opposition criticizing him, and indeed if the minister were an NDP minister of Indian affairs, he would be defending the public servants who are under attack and cannot defend themselves in the House. That is how obvious it is that this type of charge can be made for political exploitation, but it is purely ritualistic and has no substance. We all know, if the roles were changed, what they would be saying in the House if public servants were charged in this way.
This is why I find it so unfortunate that we, as adult politicians, resort to a rather phony process and ritual through which we go each time the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development come up in the standing committee or are debated in the House.
I could go through other areas which some hon. members raised about staff, for example. I think the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) asked about teachers, and so on. I will send him figures tomorrow which clearly show, without boring the House, that there has been a diminution in the staff of my department. I realize how obviously disillusioning it would be if we took a teacher from the Department of Indian Affairs and transferred him to an Indian band to take over an educational program, and then said that it was a reduction in our staff. Taking away that factor, there has been a diminution in the staff of the Department of Indian Affairs.
I opened my remarks by complimenting the committee on its work. As some hon. members have mentioned, I visited the James Bay area. When I returned I assigned one of my major advisers in the department, Mr. Tait, to follow through on the matter, to visit the communities, and to assess the James Bay areement, not in its strict legal context. I already had legal opinions. If we wanted to take it from a strictly legal point of view, it would be very difficult to establish in any court that there has been a breach with respect to federal obligations under the James Bay agreement. That was not the preoccupation of the committee, as I understood it. Certainly it was not

June 17, 1982

my preoccupation as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I am concerned with trying to deal, to the best of my ability, in an equitable and fair manner with the native people of the country. If they clearly perceive that an agreement is not fair or is not being implemented in a fair and equitable manner, because we are taking advantage of legal technicalities to their deprivation, it discredits governments generally and is unfortunate. Of course it is something which should be avoided.
I asked Mr. Tait to look at it from the perspective of the spirit of the agreement, whether the general intent as opposed to the legal interpretation had not been lived up to in any way.
I asked him-and it was not a very hard, objective standard by which to assess an agreement-to do the best he could and to try to assess where there were shortcomings within the terms of reference. Also I asked him to try to put a dollar figure on it and to try to rectify the situation, so that basically more moneys could flow to the communities to improve the health conditions to which the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) referred and many other areas referred to in the agreement.
That exercise took a long time. There is no doubt about it. He had to assess the situation and to report. I directed that the report be sent in draft form to Bill Diamond, the Grand Chief of the Cree, and to Charlie Watt of the Inuit people. I wanted them to see whether they felt that the report was a reasonable one. I wanted them to suggest changes which, hopefully, we would be prepared to adopt. It was to and fro with the draft before I took it to cabinet.
I went to cabinet. I assessed the costs. I have been working it out with my colleagues as to where we could find the money. All hon. members will be glad to hear that the process is just about completed. I hope to be in a position in the forthcoming week to ten days to meet with the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Gingras), with Billy Diamond and with the Inuit people to resolve the matter. I should like to thank all hon. members for their help. I think it is a real achievement.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
On the economic development front, I can only say that there has been some very real achievement. The Indian people have said to me-and I do not know what they have been saying to a lot of opposition members-that the panacea, almost in those strong terms, for all social ills from which they suffer is economic development. The social ills from which they suffer, such as alcoholism and the spin-off deleterious effects of unemployment-demoralization, marital life problems and so on-could be corrected overnight in a preventive way rather than in a curative way after the damage is done, if emphasis were placed upon economic development so that Indians, through their own initiative, could create jobs and employment. That is the area upon which they would like emphasis placed in terms of correcting the many social problems identified by hon. members today in the House. Indeed, these problems were identified in the document dealing with Indian conditions which I
Supply
published when 1 first became minister. I am talking about high mortality rates, high suicidal rates and so on. These are all signs of the stark and abysmal poverty of the Indian people in some parts of the country.
We have seen the commitment and will of the goverment to do something about it. Perhaps we could talk in positive terms with respect to our native people. We have indicated that we are prepared to commit moneys to native economic development. There were such moneys included in the budget of October. Over the next four years, in addition to the moneys which are already committed in the estimates of our department, $345 million is committed for the native people of Canada. This is a major commitment and it is indicative-
I regret to interrupt the hon. minister but his allotted time has expired. He will need unanimous consent of the House to continue. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I thank hon. members. I might indicate that that money will be added to $8 million for last year for major imperative projects and an additional $5 million this year. Also there are the ongoing programs in the department. I am talking about an approximate $8 million to $10 million in direct guaranteed loans for economic development. There is a $35 million contribution in terms of economic development moneys which we have already allotted. They are not counted in the $345 million, or in the special allocation of $8 million to $10 million, or in support services of $15 million. We are now getting some substantial money to put emphasis upon the much-needed area of economic development.
Let me touch upon another area to which hon. members referred, the area of education. Some native people would like us to touch upon some of the positive areas rather than the negative ones constantly and incessantly. There has been very impressive upgrading of standards and achievement by native peoples in the educational area. There are now more than
10,000	students and 157 band-operated schools. We expect- and the figures show that it is true-that the enrolment will reach at least 20,000 by 1986. Similar impressive improvements are being made in post-secondary enrolment. As recently as 1969 only about 800 Indians, as opposed to the present
10,000,	were pursuing courses in post-secondary education. This is something from which all of us can take some satisfaction. Indeed, we congratulate native people for placing emphasis upon the educational system. It is some reflection of our desire and commitment of funds to provide the facilities for them to achieve those much needed numbers.
I can only conclude by again indicating in terms of equity and fairness the tremendous emphasis which has been put on comprehensive and specific claims in the last two years as well as much added expenditures by this government over what has ever been done in the past. I am also talking about my immediate predecessor government. Negotiators have been put in place in all the comprehensive claims north of 60 and they

June 17, 1982
Supply
have been given the research moneys. When 1 first became minister there were no negotiators in place. There was very little research money to allow them to even approach a state of readiness to negotiate as well as to settle any specific claims made by the provinces, such as the most recent claims by British Columbia and the maritimes.
I could go on with a list of accomplishments but just let me say that, with the commitment now in place in the Canada Act to the recognition of treaty and aboriginal rights plus the political will shown in the allocation of needed funds to meet the priorities of the native people, perhaps we have entered a new era. Perhaps more has been done and more emphasis has been placed on the concerns of the native people in the last year and a half to two years by this government than in any other comparable period in the history of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Summarize.

I will have to. First, I come from a riding which has a very substantive native population. Indeed, I think that in terms of the global and the native community it is a very fortunate and successful community which has good selfgovernment. I think that some wonderful Canadian citizens are coming out of the universities and other institutions who were produced by that community.
Now that the Liberal Party is so proud of the negotiations that were started by my colleague, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), in terms of the settlement in the Penticton cut-off case, I would hope that they could now proceed with the IR No. 5 lands cut-off problem because we could not proceed with that in the thirty-first Parliament until the Penticton matter had been settled and that process of evaluation had been established.
In his address, the minister spoke rather extensively of the legal point of view. I suppose it is because of his professional background. He talks of spirt and legal intent. It is this area of communication between the Canadian community at large and the communities of our native people, particularly with the community and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, with which I have some concern. I keep repeating that Solzhenitsyn, in addressing the western world, has warned us about what we are getting into as we increasingly drift into a legalistic type of society where everything becomes dependent upon legal interpretation. As I see it, a behavioural and attitudinal problem has developed within the department that is at odds with what I have always considered to be the Canadian sense of fair play and morals and the rough give and take of the business community.
Since I have been a member I have had to deal with the economic development that has been attempted in Bella Coola where an entrepreneur builds a marine way and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development builds a
June 17, 1982

marine way beside it, and neither are economic so they collapse. Another example is a hotel being built by one entrepreneur and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development building another hotel, and both collapsing because of being uneconomical.
I have had to deal with the Ehattesaht matter where the department poured $5 million into a logging operation, which was a very sound economic development project for the Indian community. However, the students were paid the full trade rates in the forest industry so that within six months $5 million went down the drain and $1.7 million of receivables were lost by the industrial community around it.
If there is to be economic development in the Indian community, which I agree with the minister is their way out of many of the social and human problems they have, surely we must apply the basic rules of the marketplace and the balance sheet to that area.
I have arrived at the minister's point on legalistic terms and sense of legal intent. The minister wrote me a letter on April 29 concerning the Toussowasket problem. In my riding there is an engineering and contracting firm which has gone into receivership as a result of the legalistic games that have been played by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the band chief in the area. Donaldson Engineering Company is a firm in my riding which has now gone bankrupt and had received a Supreme Court judgment against Toussowasket Enterprises. The minister wrote me a letter telling me to have that firm proceed, that another $300,000 had been arranged to be paid to the band, and that the FDBD receivership claim, which was prior, had been paid off, so my constituent could proceed. I went to seek legal opinion on how accurate, on a legal basis, the minister's letter telling us to proceed was. I could not believe the game had been played. Obviously, a good part of my time here has been used up to prevent me from putting on the record the disgusting game, in terms of legal technique, that has been played to avoid the settlement of a Supreme Court judgment on behalf of a contractor who had performed legitimate and complete work in the Westbank Indian Band, Toussowasket Enterprises. The band chief, with the assistance of the legal department of this government has created the shell behind which there are no assets on which that judgment can be made. It has been done in one of the most shameful ways that I have ever witnessed in a lifetime in business. I have never in my life seen such legal trickery being used. I am sorry I have to use such extreme language, but I did not have enough time to put this properly on the record of the House. If I have been extreme, it has been because of the pressure of time. I see that it is ten o'clock and my time is up.
