subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR SEVERER PROVISIONS AGAINST PROSTITUTION
CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR SEVERER PROVISIONS AGAINST PROSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week, I put a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) regarding a matter that is causing some concern to a number of mayors in Canada, namely, soliciting for the purpose of prostitution. For some weeks we have been receiving letters from the mayors of various municipalities including Vancouver, Niagara and the Quebec City area, urging us to amend the Criminal Code so as to make this a more serious offence and thus enable the police to carry out more arrests.
Mr. Speaker, it is my humble opinion that our mayors are making a serious mistake if they want to use the Criminal Code in order to correct a situation that is causing traffic problems or a disturbance on the sidewalks of their municipalities. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think we have seen that there are a number of activities that take place on municipal sidewalks and these may include selling religious objects, selling other products that are not altogether legal, such as drugs, or soliciting with a view to prostitution, and I think that if we want to use the Criminal Code to regulate all the activities that take place on these sidewalks, the Code is, in my view, sufficiently clear in this respect. In any case, in one case in Alberta, in Calgary the Westendorp case which is now before the Supreme Court of Alberta, the municipal bylaw of the city of Calgary which prohibited activities related to prostitution on sidewalks was upheld. Mr. Speaker, that is why I am opposed at this time to any changes in the legislation and in the Criminal Code. I feel that, now we have adopted a charter of rights which guarantees equal rights for women, we cannot allow this kind of discrimination, which has already been with us for too long, to continue.
Recently in this House, we tabled a report on battered women and we know what the response of some of our colleagues was in this House. Statistics also show that two thirds of working women in Canada are paid the minimum wage. Then, I ask myself this question. Why should we victimize any further these women who, whatever we may say are practising a profession as old as the world itself and which was not of their own choosing? Reports of inquiries all indicate that these women are exploited persons, that they are victims and more cruelly beaten than the others. These women are at the mercy of people who exploit them as far as drugs and money are concerned. They are the victims and we want them today to be still more victimized.

June 17, 1982
Adjournment Debate
1 think, Mr. Speaker, that we are shifting the problem and when I referred to the statistics provided by Statistics Canada on offences dealing with prostitution, the legislation was amended in 1972, and since 1972, I noted that there has been no dramatic change. Indeed, from 1976 to 1980, there has been a decrease in the volume of offences and I think this is merely due to the fact that the law is not enforced. Moreover, as I mentioned it to some of the mayors in connection with other activities such as pornography in public places such as theatres and elsewhere, there are no statistics on arrests, no offences reported. The number of reported offences with respect to pornography is so low that the Canadian statistics do not even take them into account. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I wanted in the first place to point out to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) the views of several women's organizations which appeared before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs whose proceedings unfortunately are not televised.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we have sections in the Criminal Code that deal with indecent acts, nudity, loitering, disturbing the peace, procuring, bawdy houses. For procuring we have penalties up to 10 years, and looking at the statistics in that area, out of 1,520 charges laid, 60 males and 18 females were arrested in 1980. Where are all the people exploiting Canadian women in such distress, what did the provincial governments do? What do municipalities intend to do? I would invite all those prudish mayors and authorities, all those police officers, all the people charged with enforcing the law, to look at the Criminal Code and find out that sections dealing with these matters are already in it. Section 195.1 already deals with soliciting and arrests can be made. But let us not prohibit women from walking the streets thus increasing discrimination. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I hope the committee on justice and legal affairs and also the Minister of Justice will at least and at best maintain the section as it is. And if we have any courage, let us recommend that this House repeal that section because I feel that those who exploit that trade should be very severely punished. Our statistics should not report for a whole year in Canada only 60 cases of people convicted of such a serious offence, as exploiting. In other countries mention is made of white slavery. These things happen to young people. Currently I am told that in Vancouver, young people are involved. The Young Offenders' Act provides for severe penalties for abduction of a minor, and 1 wonder what provincial attorneys general are doing, 1 wonder what provincial authorities are doing, what police officers and judges are doing in those cases.
Looking at statistics I tell myself that once again we are the most victimized members of society, and it is not by changing the law or by putting teeth into it that we will correct the
problem. I see that what concerns our colleagues is a case heard in British Columbia, where a police officer used as bait could not get one of those girls convicted. The facts of the case are clear, I think that the police officer simply did not do his job properly or should have been better informed, because I think that if we want to enforce the act as it is, it is very easy to do, but let us not be hypocritical and tell people that because this is a federal act and the Criminal Code, that the federal government is doing nothing in this matter when in fact the blame should be put on local authorities.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Therese Killens (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR SEVERER PROVISIONS AGAINST PROSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien), I shall reply this evening to a question asked by the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette), who has just spoken on the same subject. Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Justice told the hon. member in the House yesterday, members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs are now considering the issue of solicitation for the purposes of prostitution. As a member of this committee, I have myself attended all the proceedings on this matter and on Bill C-53.
As the hon. member has just stated, the mayors of Vancouver, Calgary and Niagara Falls, as well as the mayor of Etobicoke, in his capacity as Chairman of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Commission, have appeared before the committee. On the one hand, Mr. Speaker, the mayor of Vancouver asks that the Criminal Code be amended. He would like the offence of solicitation not have to be qualified as insistent or persistent. He would also like the customers who solicit prostitutes to be charged, but on the other hand, the mayors of Calgary and Niagara Falls would be happy to have the problem dealt with by municipal bylaws. The mayor of Calgary even urged the members of the committee to do whatever is necessary to guarantee that these bylaws cannot be considered ultra vires.
Finally, the Supreme Court of Canada has granted authorization to appeal the issue of the legality of the Calgary bylaw, and this appeal will be heard only in September, 1982. According to the testimony, it seems that the municipal bylaws of Calgary, Niagara Falls and Vancouver deal effectively with prostitutes and their clients, whether men or women.
To my knowledge, no change in the section of the code which deals with this matter has yet been suggested to the members of the committee, in the event it should be established that this section no longer meets present needs. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the hon. members that the committee is still considering ways to settle this difficult issue and that it should be able to comment on it and to bring forward suggestions by next fall.
June 17, 1982

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ROLE OF PAROLE BOARD OFFICER. (B) NATURE OF SUPERVISION
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ROLE OF PAROLE BOARD OFFICER. (B) NATURE OF SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise tonight to speak about a very serious matter. I know all members of the House agree it is serious. I think it is appropriate for me to point out the question 1 raise is within the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) who, and this is quite an uncommon occurrence, but one I commend, is here tonight. I understand he will be replying to my remarks. I know the Solicitor General is here because he is deeply concerned about the matter my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), and I raised on Monday. It concerns the terrible case of a man named Kocurek who was convicted recently in British Columbia of the killing of a 15-year-old girl on August 2, 1981. The tragedy, and that is all that it can be described as-a terrible tradegy-is made more terrible by the fact that Kocurek was out at the time on what is called mandatory supervision.
Kocurek had been convicted of indecent assault on a four-year-old girl, but after he had served two-thirds of his sentence, he was out on mandatory supervision. As pointed out by the Solicitor General, this is a matter of law. It is very interesting that the federal authorities are reported in the press as having said that Kocurek could not have received ordinary parole because he was considered dangerous. He was denied parole, apparently, because reports said he liked to choke women during the sex act. One psychiatrist's report warned that he would kill if he went untreated. He was released on June 22, 1981, as the Solicitor General knows, after he had served two thirds of his sentence. I agree with the Solicitor General that in law that was all that could happen. He had to be released, but justice officials then warned provincial authorities and the local mental health authorities that, and I quote from a press release:
Kocurek should be carefully monitored and reports made to his parole officer.
Unfortunately and tragically, when he missed his appointment at the mental health clinic, apparently nobody told the federal authorities. Apparently the federal parole authorities were not able to keep close enough supervision on Kocurek, so his activities were not in fact monitored.
The matter of mandatory supervision has been raised before, and 1 want to remind hon. members that on October 29, 1981, the Solicitor General said in answer to a question in relation to mandatory supervision put by my Conservative colleague, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
When I got the study in July-
This was in relation to a study on mandatory supervision.
-I circulated it through the criminal justice constituency across the country. I indicated that 1 would wait until the end of October for their comments on these recommendations.
That was October of last year.
Adjournment Debate
I expect to close the book on receiving comments from these groups shortly. I hope that within a few months I will be able to go to cabinet with proposals for change and for improving the mandatory supervision system.
Later, on January 27, 1982, another colleague in my party, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), raised the matter with the Solicitor General, and the Solicitor General said, as recorded in Hansard:
-and I am planning to go to cabinet shortly with proposals for change.
On June 14 the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and I raised this matter in the House. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra asked:
Why was Kocurek allowed to be lawfully at large, carrying a pistol and handcuffs, after failing to show up for his first scheduled visit to the mental health unit?
Then 1 asked:
Was there in fact a parole board officer to whom Kocurek was supposed to report? If there was, why was that parole board officer not keeping track of what Kocurek was supposed to be doing? I refer especially to his refusal to turn up at the mental health clinic? Why did no one know about this?
The Solicitor General replied:
-I would like to have the opportunity to look into that further before answering the question.
It is interesting that a paper was delivered on November 13, 1981, by Graham Stewart, the executive director of the John Howard Society of Kingston. With respect to mandatory supervision he said:
I would like to add here that in addition to mandatory supervision not being able to either offer control or substantial assistance, the report acknowledges that staff involved in the mandatory supervision are not able to identify those who are likely to be dangerous even if they could assert this control.
It may or may not be appropriate to maintain mandatory supervision-I am inclined to think that it is not-but what is certainly of importance is that as long as it is maintained in the law, and I understand the difficulties the Solicitor General has with this because it is mandatory, then surely he can do something to tighten up the so-called supervision that goes with it.
I know the Solicitor General is deeply concerned about this case and others, as are the people in the part of British Columbia in which this happened, and as are all hon. members. I would ask the Solicitor General to give us some assurance tonight that the report to which he referred many months ago will be dealt with. I know it takes time to get cabinet decisions but I hope that even before that is forthcoming the Solicitor General can give us some assurance that supervision is taking place and will continue to take place. I hope he will do more than tighten up the system, but will improve it considerably.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ROLE OF PAROLE BOARD OFFICER. (B) NATURE OF SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the kind words said about me by my hon. friend. In three short minutes I should like to talk about this case and, what is more important, about the system of mandatory supervision.

June 17, 1982
Adjournment Debate
As 1 said I would, 1 have inquired into the matter and have learned that Kocurek was reporting to a parole officer. He was supposed to report every two weeks and he did. Between his reports there were telephone calls. I can assure the hon. member that if there had been any knowledge at all of the alleged facts-that he was carrying handcuffs and a fire arm with him-he would have been in violation of his mandatory supervision and it would have been suspended.
In addition, he was to report for psychiatric attention regularly. He missed one of those appearances and phoned the mental health unit to inform them that he had the flu. That may well have been true-he may well have had the flu. No further check was made into the claim that he had the flu and before any further visits were to take place, the tragic murder occurred.
A terrible dilemma is presented by dangerous offenders who are reaching the end of their sentence. The simple fact is that as they reach the end of their sentence it becomes inevitable, because the sentence is limited, that they will be on the street. The question which is presented to society and the question upon which I ask my hon. friend to reflect and upon which he will be called to vote when, shortly, I hope, tougher legislation will be introduced in connection with mandatory supervision, is do we as a society get a better handle on these dangerous offenders by having a period of time when they are on the street but still under warrant? In these circumstances they could be watched and be subject to conditions and be guided by psychiatrists, social workers and parole officers.
On the other hand, is it better to keep them in until the very end of their sentence? I wonder if the extra eight or nine months of incarceration, which is about the average, would make them less dangerous or less of a threat? Is it better to keep them in until society has no more right to claim their attention or give them direction, and then let them out cold turkey into society?
We have always had the theory in our country, because we have had early release for decades, that it is better to get the individual into the street for some period of time, recognizing the risks but having the benefit of being able to control and direct them. That is one of the arguments for mandatory supervision and I ask my hon. friend to reflect on that when my proposals are brought forward, which proposals preserve mandatory supervision but considerably toughen it up.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) a question about the CN announcement of lay-offs in Tran-scona, Point St. Charles and Moncton. At that time CN announced a six to eight-week shutdown in addition to the usual summer shutdown; six on the "motive" power side and eight on the car side. Since then the lay-offs have been extended to ten weeks past the summer shutdown, thus adding to the problems of many of my constituents who work in those shops,
and further compromising the role of the CN as a service and not just any other out-for-a-quick-buck business enterprise.
In answer, the minister said that it was not his policy to interfere in the day to day affairs of CN. I reminded him that he did not have any qualms about interfering in the activities of VIA Rail when he saw fit, and surely the lay-off of thousands of people could not be rightfully regarded as simply a day to day activity. Now, when he has the opportunity to do something intelligent with regard to the railways, he sits on his hands and says it is none of his business.
The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that it is his business. The CN acts upon the instructions of the government, and since 1975 has been instructed by the Liberals to make a profit at all costs. Indeed, up until 1982, it was doing just that. Then, because of traffic reduction and subsequent revenue loss-thanks in part to the economic mismanagement of the Liberals themselves-it has not made a profit and this has led to the lay-offs; not because there was no work or no future for the railway, not because there will be no need for the equipment which will go unrepaired during the lay-off, but only because they did not make a profit. In my view, this is the ultimate in shortsightedness and social irresponsibility; the kind of thing only Conservatives could be happy with. By that I mean the Tories have always wanted Crown corporations like CN to operate only according to profit and to hell with the lives of the workers.
I have nothing against an efficiently run railroad, Mr. Speaker. All railroaders want to feel they are part of an efficient and admirable enterprise. To this extent they also have been glad that the CN has redeemed itself in the public eye, even though most of its historic debt was due to inheritance rather than operating deficit. But no one is in favour of the short-term profit motive when it comes to transportation. Transportation is not a need which is going to go away; it will always be with us. The railway will always be an important part of that transportation system, especially as we move into the energy-scarce future.
The CN must be given the money it needs for capital expansion and expansion in general, but this money must not come from Canadian farmers through changes in the Crow rate, or from railway workers themselves in the form of layoffs. It should come from general revenues as an investment by the Government of Canada in the future of this country, a future in which the Canadian National and other Crown corporations will be used as instruments of the public interest and not as isolated meaningless profit centres.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members are aware of the facts. Faced with a first quarter loss-not a profit as the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) would lead the public to believe-of $34.7 million and no immediate improvement in the economic outlook, CN Rail announced an extended close down of its three main shops, in Moncton,
June 17, 1982

Montreal and Winnipeg. The close down will be in addition to the normal four week summer break, July 12 to August 6, 1982, and will affect locomotive and freight car repair operations. Both operations will re-open October 15.
Lay-offs in the railway industry as a result of a decline in traffic have taken place before and are not considered an unusual response in times of slow economic activity. For example, in 1975, CP temporarily laid off 3,000 workers for seven weeks in the post-holiday period. In 1977, CN instituted a four-week extension to the normal holiday period for some workers.
The hon. member said that workers could be working and repairing existing equipment. At the moment, CN has 240 locomotives and 8,000 freight cars sitting idle. I am confident that CN is maintaining its fleet adequately. It is simply a case of there being fewer cars and locomotives to maintain.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext: Not all those cars are repaired. Eight thousand are waiting for repair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext:
I am surprised that the hon. member encouraged the minister to interfere in CN operations by directing it to cancel the lay-offs. As the minister explained to the hon. member, the role of a minister with respect to Crown corporations is to indicate general policy guidelines. It is not to dictate
Adjournment Debate
how many people should be laid off over what period of time. He did not say, as the hon. member mentioned tonight, that it was none of his business. That is not what he said at all. He said his role is to set policy. Why have Crown corporations if the minister is going to be involved in the day-to-day operations of these Crown corporations?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext: 1 am complaining about policy.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) NOTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext: Decisions regarding lay-offs are not easy ones to take and are not taken lightly by railway management.
